name: Ground Mats
h1: Equipment Mats and Ground Protection Mats
title: Equipment Mats for Sale: Ground Protection Mats
meta: Equipment mats for sale for tree crews: ground protection mats that keep bucket trucks, chippers and loaders from rutting lawns, turf and soft ground.
intro: Equipment mats spread the weight of bucket trucks, mini loaders and chippers so you can get to the tree without tearing up a customer's lawn. Ground protection mats also give outriggers a firmer footing on soft or wet ground.

p: Size the mats to the machine and the access route. Smaller mats like a 3x8 are easy for one or two people to handle and work well for compact loaders and walk-behind gear. Heavier trucks and long runs across turf call for more mats laid end to end, so plan on enough to leapfrog as you move.

Look for a tread pattern on both sides for traction, molded handholds for carrying, and a way to link mats together on longer runs. Rinse them at the end of the job and check for cracks before they go back on the truck. Outrigger pads are still the right tool directly under outriggers; mats are for travel paths and staging areas.

Lay the route before the machines arrive and walk it once to spot sprinkler heads, septic lids, soft spots and buried edging. Overlap or link mats so wheels and tracks never drop off an edge, and avoid sharp turns on the mats, which is where most turf damage happens.

On wet clay or a soggy lawn, mats are often what makes the job possible at all. They also cut cleanup time, because you are not raking ruts and reseeding at the end of the day. Stack them flat on the trailer and strap them down; loose mats in the wind are dangerous.

faq.q: Can ground protection mats go under bucket truck outriggers?
faq.a: Mats help on access routes, but outriggers should sit on pads rated for that use and set up per the truck manufacturer's instructions. Use mats to protect the path in and out.

name: Chainsaw Accessories
title: Chainsaw Accessories: Bars, Chain, Chaps, Fuel & Tools
meta: Chainsaw accessories for arborists and loggers: bars and chain, chaps and pants, cases, fuel and oil, felling wedges, files and wrenches for daily saw work.
intro: Chainsaw accessories are the supplies that keep a saw cutting and a crew protected: replacement bars and chain, chaps and chainsaw pants, cases, premixed fuel and bar oil, felling wedges, files and wrenches. This department collects the chainsaw tools and supplies a tree crew goes through every week.

p: Start with the cutting system. Keep at least one spare chain for every saw on the truck, and a spare bar for the saws you run hardest. Match the replacement bar and chain to the saw's pitch, gauge and drive-link count, which are stamped on the bar or listed in the owner's manual. Getting one of the three wrong means the chain will not fit or will not run safely.

Next is maintenance: a scrench or bar wrench sized for your bar nuts, round files in the right diameter for your chain, a flat file and depth gauge tool for the rakers. A few minutes of sharpening at lunch saves more fuel and frustration than any other habit on a saw crew.

Organize the saw kit so every saw has its own wrench, file and spare chain in a box or pouch that travels with it. When a climber sends a saw down for a sharp chain, the ground worker should be able to make the swap in a minute without hunting.

Anyone running a saw on the ground should wear chainsaw-resistant leg protection, either chaps or chainsaw pants. Chaps are cheaper and easy to share across a crew; pants are more comfortable for full days and for climbers who come down to buck. Either way, replace them once the protective layer has been cut, because the fibers that stop a chain only work once.

A hard case or bar scabbard protects the chain and the truck bed, and keeps the bar from catching a leg when you carry the saw through brush. Cases also keep bar oil off the seats when a saw rides in the cab.

Premixed ethanol-free fuel is more expensive per gallon but helps saws that sit between jobs start reliably and avoids mixing errors. If you mix your own, use a quality two-stroke oil at the ratio the saw maker specifies and a clearly labeled can. Keep bar and chain oil topped off every tank of fuel.

For felling and bucking, plastic felling wedges are a must. Carry a few sizes so you can stack them, and drive them with an axe or a wedge hammer rather than the saw. Wedges keep a bar from pinching and give you control over where a stem goes.

Common chainsaw attachments include bar tip guards, chain catchers, spike bumpers and lanyard rings for top-handle saws. Only fit parts made for your saw model, and never remove the chain brake, chain catcher or other factory safety features. When in doubt, check the owner's manual or a servicing dealer.

Chainsaw supplies like spare starter rope, spark plugs and air filters belong in the same box. They are cheap, and having them on hand keeps a saw running when the nearest dealer is an hour away. Restock after every week so the truck never runs out of the basics.

faq.q: What chainsaw accessories should a new arborist buy first?
faq.a: Chaps or chainsaw pants, a spare chain, the right round file and guide, a bar wrench, felling wedges and a case. Add premixed fuel and a spare bar once you know which saws you run most.

faq.q: How do I know which bar and chain fit my saw?
faq.a: Check the pitch, gauge and drive-link count stamped on your current bar or listed in the manual. A replacement bar must also match the saw's mount pattern.

faq.q: How often should chainsaw chaps be replaced?
faq.a: Replace them as soon as a chain has cut into the protective layer, and when they are worn, contaminated with fuel or oil, or past the manufacturer's service guidance.

faq.q: Are aftermarket chainsaw attachments safe?
faq.a: Use only accessories designed for your specific saw, follow the manufacturer's instructions, and never remove factory safety features such as the chain brake or chain catcher.

name: Bars & Chain
title: Chainsaw Bar and Chain: Replacement Bars & Saw Chain
meta: Chainsaw bar and chain replacements for pro saws: guide bars in common lengths plus full-comp and semi-chisel chain matched by pitch, gauge and drive links.
intro: A chainsaw bar and chain wear together, and replacing them as a matched set keeps a pro saw cutting straight. Browse replacement bars and saw chain by pitch and gauge for the saws arborists and loggers run.

guide.h: Matching a replacement bar and chain
p: Three numbers decide fit: pitch (such as .325 or 3/8), gauge (such as .050 or .063) and drive-link count. The bar also has to match the saw's mount. Find these on the bar tail or in the manual before you order.

Lightweight laminated bars suit top-handle and mid-size saws used in the tree, while solid bars hold up better on big saws in the log. A new chain on a worn bar will run crooked, so flip the bar regularly, dress the rails, and replace the sprocket every couple of chains.

Most bar and chain trouble starts with oil and tension. Check that the oiler is putting a line of oil on a stump when you rev the saw, clean the oil hole and bar groove every time you change chains, and set tension so the chain snaps back against the bar but still pulls freely by hand.

Flip the bar each time you sharpen so both rails wear evenly, and file off any burr on the rail edges. If the chain leans to one side in the groove or the saw starts cutting in a curve, the rails are uneven or the chain is filed unevenly. Keep a couple of matched bar and chain sets on the truck so a pinched or damaged bar does not end the day.

faq.q: Should I replace the bar and chain at the same time?
faq.a: Not always, but a badly worn bar or sprocket will chew up a new chain. Check rail wear and the sprocket whenever you put on a fresh chain.

name: Chainsaw Bars
title: Chainsaw Bars: Light, Laminated & Replacement Guide Bars
meta: Chainsaw bars for arborists: lightweight and laminated replacement guide bars matched to pitch, gauge and saw mount, from top-handle saws to big felling saws.
intro: Chainsaw bars take a beating on every cut, and a straight bar with good rails is what makes a sharp chain cut true. These replacement chain saw bars cover common pitches and gauges for pro saws.

p: Run the shortest bar that does the job. A shorter bar is lighter in the tree, easier to control and less prone to kickback. Lightweight bars save real weight on saws you carry all day; solid and laminated bars handle abuse better in rough bucking.

Match pitch, gauge, drive-link count and the saw's mount pattern. Some customers search for a bow bar for a chainsaw; bow bars are a specialty cutting attachment and are not appropriate for tree work, so we stick to standard guide bars.

A bar is worn out when the rails are low, chipped or spread, when the groove is too shallow to hold the drive links square, or when the nose sprocket is loose or rough. Pinching a bar in a cut can bend it; sight down the bar and replace it if it is not straight.

Clean the groove and oil holes with each chain change, grease the nose sprocket if the bar has a grease port, and flip the bar regularly. Running a lighter bar on a climbing saw saves real effort over a full day aloft, while a sturdier bar is the better buy for the ground saw that sees dirt, stumps and pinches.

faq.q: How do I measure a chainsaw bar?
faq.a: Bar length is measured from the front of the saw body to the tip of the cutter. The called length is rounded to the nearest inch, so use the stamped part info when ordering.

name: Saw Chain
title: Chainsaw Chain: Full-Comp & Semi-Chisel Saw Chain
meta: Chainsaw chain for pro saws: full-comp and semi-chisel loops in 3/8 and .325 pitch, .050 and .063 gauge. Match the chain to your bar before you order.
intro: Chainsaw chain is a consumable on any tree crew, and a stack of sharp loops on the truck keeps the day moving. Choose full-chisel style cutters for speed in clean wood or semi-chisel for dirty, frozen or abrasive work.

p: Pitch and gauge must match the bar and sprocket, and the drive-link count must match the bar length. Full-comp chain has a cutter on every other link for the fastest cut; semi-chisel cutters hold an edge longer in dirty wood and are more forgiving to sharpen.
File with the correct round file diameter for your chain and keep the depth gauges set. A dull chain makes dust instead of chips, pulls the saw into the wood and wears the bar.

Touch up the cutters with a few file strokes every tank or two, keeping the same angle and number of strokes on each tooth. Check the depth gauges every few sharpenings; too high and the saw will not bite, too low and it grabs and kicks. A chain is done when the cutters are worn back to the manufacturer's minimum or when teeth are cracked or broken.

Rotating several chains through a sprocket keeps wear even. When a chain hits a rock or nail, swap it out and have it ground rather than trying to fix it with a file on the stump. A sharp chain is the best safety and productivity upgrade most crews can make.

faq.q: What chain should a climber run on a top-handle saw?
faq.a: Most climbers run a narrow-kerf or low-profile chain in the pitch the saw ships with. Stick to the chain types the saw manufacturer lists for that model.

name: Saw Cases
title: Chainsaw Cases: Hard Cases and Bar Scabbards
meta: Chainsaw cases and scabbards that protect the bar, chain and truck: hard carrying cases for pro saws and bar covers for moving saws around the job site.
intro: Chainsaw cases keep a saw clean, contain bar oil and protect the chain on the ride between jobs. A good chain saw case is also safer to carry through brush than a bare bar.

p: A full hard case protects the whole saw and keeps oil off seats and other gear, which matters if saws ride in a cab or an enclosed trailer. Check the listed bar length the case fits before you buy.

A bar scabbard covers just the bar and chain. It is lighter and quicker on and off for saws that go in and out of the truck all day. Use one any time you carry a saw through a crowd of crew or customers.

guide.h: Getting the most from a chainsaw case
p: Drain or tighten fuel and oil caps before a saw goes in a case, and let a hot saw cool before closing the lid. Clean sawdust out of the case now and then so it does not hold moisture against the bar.

Cases with room for a file, wrench and spare chain keep a saw kit together, which helps on jobs where saws get handed around. For saws that ride in an open truck bed, a case also cuts down on dings to the handle and covers. Label cases by saw if your crew runs several of the same model.

faq.q: Will a chainsaw case fit a longer bar?
faq.a: Only up to its listed bar length. A longer bar will not close in the case and can damage the chain.

name: Chaps & Pants
h1: Chainsaw Chaps and Arborist Chainsaw Pants
title: Chainsaw Chaps & Arborist Chainsaw Pants
meta: Arborist chainsaw pants and chainsaw chaps for sale: leg protection for ground saw work, from apron chaps for the whole crew to cooler full-day saw pants.
intro: Arborist chainsaw pants and chainsaw chaps are the leg protection every ground saw operator needs. Choose shareable apron chaps for the crew or fitted pants for people who run a saw all day.

p: Chaps strap over work pants, fit a range of sizes and are the economical choice for a crew. Chainsaw pants put the protective layer inside a fitted pant, so they move better on long days and when climbers come down to buck and chip.
Look for protection that meets ASTM F1897 or carries a UL listing, and pick a length that covers from the hip to the boot top. Replace chaps or pants once the protective fibers have been cut.

Leg protection only works if it covers the right area and stays in place. Chaps should reach from the waist to the boot top and buckle snugly behind the leg. Pants should be long enough to overlap the boots without bunching. Try a high step and a squat before the first job.

Wash according to the label, keep fuel and bar oil off the fabric, and inspect for cuts after each day. Do not patch cut protection; replace it. Lighter, vented fabrics are worth the extra money in summer, because PPE that is too hot to wear ends up in the truck instead of on the saw operator.

faq.q: Do climbers need chainsaw pants?
faq.a: Requirements vary by situation and employer, but anyone running a saw on the ground should wear leg protection. Many climbers wear saw pants so they are covered when they come down.

name: Chainsaw Chaps
title: Chainsaw Chaps: Apron & Full-Wrap Chainsaw Safety Chaps
meta: Chainsaw chaps for tree crews and homeowners: apron-style chainsaw safety chaps that block a moving chain, plus tips on sizing, standards and when to replace.
intro: Chainsaw chaps are the simplest way to protect your legs when you run a saw on the ground. These chain saw chaps strap over your work pants and use layers of long fibers that pull out and jam the sprocket when a chain contacts them.

p: Under the tough outer shell, chaps have several layers of long, loosely woven fibers. When a moving chain cuts the shell, those fibers are dragged into the drive sprocket and stop the chain. That is why a chap that has been cut must be retired: the fibers have done their job once.

Chaps do not make you cut-proof. They are designed to reduce injury from contact at typical saw speeds, and a saw at full throttle with a sharp chain can still cause harm. Good technique, a working chain brake and a clear work area come first.

Remember that chaps protect the front of the legs, where most saw contact happens, but a chain can still reach other areas. Keep both hands on the saw, engage the chain brake when walking, and never run a saw above shoulder height on the ground. Chaps are part of a system that includes boots, gloves, a helmet with eye and hearing protection, and training.

Apron chaps cover the front of each leg from the hip down and buckle at the back of the thigh. They are light, quick to put on and the common choice for crews. Full-wrap chaps add protection around the calf, which helps if you often work in awkward positions or around brush.

Lightweight chaps made from newer fabrics breathe better in hot weather, which makes it more likely people will actually wear them all day. Economy chaps are a good option for occasional users and spares on the truck.

If you are outfitting a crew, keep a few lengths on the truck so everyone gets chaps that actually fit. Mark each pair with its length and an in-service date. For anyone who runs a saw all day, chainsaw pants are worth considering as an upgrade, since they fit closer and move better.

Measure from the belt line to about two inches above the ankle and pick the closest length. Chaps should cover the top of your boot when you are standing. Too short leaves the shin exposed; too long and they catch on brush.

In the US, look for chaps that meet ASTM F1897 or carry a UL classification for chainsaw leg protection. ANSI Z133 expects chain-saw-resistant leg protection for ground operators, so check your employer's policy too.

Wash chaps according to the manufacturer's label; some can be machine washed and others should only be hand washed. Do not repair cuts with patches, because a patch will not restore the fibers underneath. Fuel and bar oil break down the fabric over time, so wipe off spills and store chaps dry. Replace any chap that has been cut, is badly worn or is past the maker's service life.

Inspect chaps before each use. Look for cuts through the outer shell, pulled fibers sticking out, torn straps or broken buckles, and fabric that is stiff with oil or fuel. Chaps that pass inspection should still be replaced when they reach the maker's service life.

faq.q: Do chainsaw chaps really stop a chain?
faq.a: They are designed to stop or slow a chain on contact by jamming the sprocket with fibers, which greatly reduces injury. They are not a guarantee, so treat them as the last line of defense.

faq.q: Can I wear chaps over chainsaw pants?
faq.a: You can, but it is rarely needed. Choose one or the other and make sure it covers from the hip to the boot top.

faq.q: How do I size chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: Measure from your belt line to about two inches above the ankle and choose the nearest listed length. They should overlap the top of your boots.

faq.q: Can I patch cut chainsaw chaps?
faq.a: No. Once the protective layer is cut it will not stop a chain the same way again. Replace the chaps.

name: Chainsaw Pants
title: Chainsaw Pants & Chainsaw Trousers for Arborists
meta: Chainsaw pants and chainsaw trousers for climbers and ground crews: chainsaw chap pants with built-in leg protection that stay cool and move with you all day.
intro: Chainsaw pants build the cut-resistant layer into a fitted pair of work pants, so you are protected without buckling on chaps. For people who run a saw most of the day, chainsaw trousers are more comfortable and catch less brush.

p: Check that the protective layer covers the front of the legs from the waist to the boot top, and look for ASTM F1897 or UL-classified protection. Light, ventilated pants with stretch panels are easier to climb in, while denim-look styles hold up to chipping and hauling brush.
Size them like your regular work pants but try a squat and a high step, since climbers need room at the knee. Replace pants once the protective layer has been cut, and follow the label for washing.

guide.h: Pants for climbers and ground crews
p: Climbers usually want light chainsaw pants with stretch and good knee room, since they move a lot and may only run a saw on the ground for part of the day. Ground workers who buck and chip all day often prefer heavier fabrics that stand up to brush and chips.

Look for reinforced cuffs, enough pockets for a wrench and phone, and suspender buttons if you carry tools on your belt. Chainsaw chap pants with full-length protection on the front give the most coverage. Buy a spare pair if you work every day, so one can dry while you wear the other.

faq.q: Are chainsaw pants better than chaps?
faq.a: They are more comfortable for all-day use and fit better, but cost more. Chaps are easier to share across a crew.

name: Fuel & Oil
title: Chainsaw Fuel and Oil: Premix, 2-Stroke Oil & Cans
meta: Chainsaw fuel and oil for pro saws: ethanol-free 50:1 premix, synthetic blend 2-stroke oil and safety fuel cans for storing and pouring gas on the job site.
intro: Chainsaw fuel and oil are what keep two-stroke saws running clean. Choose premixed ethanol-free fuel for convenience and storage life, or synthetic blend two-stroke oil to mix your own, plus proper cans to carry it.

p: Premixed 50:1 fuel costs more but removes mixing mistakes and stores well, so saws that sit between jobs start easily. If you mix your own, use fresh gas, a quality two-stroke oil and the ratio your saw maker specifies.

Store fuel in an approved, clearly labeled can, and keep mix separate from straight gas. A no-spill spout makes fueling cleaner and keeps gas off the saw and the ground. Refuel with the saw off and cooled, away from where you will restart it.

Fill bar and chain oil every time you fill fuel. A saw that runs dry of bar oil cooks the bar and chain in minutes. Use a dedicated bar oil rather than motor oil, and choose a winter grade when it gets cold.

Fuel cans should be clearly marked for mixed fuel and kept upright, out of the sun and away from ignition sources on the truck. Move at least the distance your crew requires away from the fueling spot before starting the saw, and wipe up spills before they reach the saw's muffler. Premixed fuel in sealed cans keeps longer than pump gas, which helps for saws that are used only now and then.

faq.q: Can I use car gas in my chainsaw?
faq.a: Many saws run on fresh unleaded with the right oil mix, but ethanol can cause problems in stored fuel. Check your owner's manual for fuel guidance.

name: Felling Wedges
title: Felling Wedges: Plastic Wedges and Logging Belt Kits
meta: Felling wedges for tree removal and bucking: plastic wedges that keep the bar from pinching and help control where a stem falls, plus a logging belt kit.
intro: Felling wedges keep the kerf open so the bar does not pinch, and they help drive a tree in the direction you planned. Plastic wedges are safe to hit with a saw chain by accident, unlike steel.

p: Carry at least two or three wedges in different sizes so you can stack them for more lift. Set them in the back cut as soon as there is room, and drive them with an axe or wedge hammer, never the saw. A belt kit keeps wedges and a tape on your hip so they are there when you need them.
Wedges are not a substitute for a proper notch, hinge and a planned escape route. On leaning or heavy trees, get training and use rigging or mechanical help as needed.

Small wedges start in a thin back cut, and larger, taller wedges give more lift once they are set. Stacking two wedges adds lift when a tree needs a push. Ribbed or textured faces help wedges stay put instead of popping out when struck.

A logging belt with a wedge pouch keeps wedges, a tape and a small axe where you can reach them while you keep a hand on the saw. Replace wedges that are cracked or badly mushroomed at the head, because they can split or fly when driven. Keep a few spares on the truck, since wedges tend to get lost in brush piles and sent through chippers.

faq.q: Why use plastic felling wedges instead of steel?
faq.a: A chain that touches a plastic wedge gets dulled; a chain that hits steel can be damaged and kick. Plastic or composite wedges are standard for saw work.

name: Wrenches & Files
title: Chainsaw Wrench, Bar Wrench & Chainsaw Files
meta: Chainsaw wrench and file supplies: bar wrenches and combination tools for bar nuts and spark plugs, plus round files sold by the dozen for sharpening chain.
intro: A chainsaw wrench and a good round file are the two tools you will reach for most. Keep a combination bar wrench in every saw kit and a supply of files sized to your chain.

guide.h: Wrenches and files for the saw kit
p: A combination wrench, often called a scrench, handles bar nuts and the spark plug, with a screwdriver tip for chain tension. Some crews call it an arbor wrench or bar wrench. Pick the size that matches your saw's bar nuts.

Round files must match the cutter size of your chain, commonly 5/32, 11/64, 3/16 or 7/32 inch. Use a file guide for consistent angles, file from the inside of the cutter out, and keep strokes even on both sides. Buying by the dozen is cheaper, and a dull file makes a dull chain.

A consistent routine beats a perfect one done once a week. Clamp the bar in a stump vise or log, set your file guide on the chain, count strokes per tooth, and work all the cutters on one side before switching. Check the depth gauges every few sharpenings with a gauge tool and a flat file.

Files are consumables. A file that skates over the tooth instead of biting is dull, and keeps going dull faster as you push harder. Buying files by the dozen keeps a fresh one in every saw kit. Clean the bar groove and check the sprocket while you sharpen, since you already have the saw on your knee.

faq.q: What size file do I need for my chain?
faq.a: It depends on pitch and chain type. Check the chain's packaging or the saw manual for the recommended file diameter.

name: Chipper Knives
title: Chipper Blades & Chipper Knives for Brush Chippers
meta: Chipper blades and chipper knives for brush chippers, including replacements sized for common Vermeer models, with tips on rotation, sharpening and swaps.
intro: Sharp chipper blades feed brush faster, burn less fuel and put less strain on the machine. These replacement chipper knives fit common brush chippers used by tree crews.

p: Check knives daily during heavy use. A dull or chipped knife makes the chipper pull poorly, chew instead of cut and send more vibration through bearings. Many knives are double-edged, so you can flip them once before sharpening.

Confirm the knife size, bolt pattern and machine model before ordering, and torque the bolts to the manufacturer's spec. Always lock out the chipper and make sure the disc or drum has fully stopped before opening the housing. Have dull knives reground by someone who can hold the original angle.

Chipper knives vary by length, width, thickness, bevel and bolt pattern, even between models from the same maker. Measure the old knife or find the part number for your chipper before ordering, and confirm whether your machine uses a matching anvil or bed knife that should be adjusted when blades are changed.

Change all knives on a disc or drum at the same time so the machine stays balanced, and use new bolts if the old ones are stretched or damaged. Keep a second set of sharp knives on hand so a swap can happen in the yard, not on a job. Never reach into a chipper housing until the machine is off, the key removed and everything has stopped.

faq.q: How often should chipper knives be changed?
faq.a: It depends on how much and what kind of material you chip. Dirt, sand and stumps dull knives fast. Inspect them daily and flip or sharpen at the first sign of poor feeding.

name: Landscaper Tools
h1: Landscaping Tools for Tree and Grounds Crews
title: Landscaping Tools: Rakes, Ladders, Sprayers & Line
meta: Landscaping tools for tree and grounds crews: cleanup rakes and replacement parts, orchard ladders, backpack sprayers and trimmer line for daily site work.
intro: Landscaping tools handle the cleanup and grounds work that comes with every tree job. Here you will find heavy rakes and replacement parts, orchard ladders, a battery backpack sprayer and trimmer line.

guide.h: Tools for cleanup and grounds work
p: A wide, stiff rake moves chips, sawdust and small brush fast, and replacement tines or handles keep a good rake in service. A steel leaf rake is the backup for finish cleanup on lawns.

Tripod orchard ladders give stable footing on uneven ground for pruning small trees and hedges; set the third leg into the canopy side and follow the ladder's duty rating. Backpack sprayers and trimmer line round out the kit for crews that also handle grounds maintenance.

Rakes with replaceable tines and handles last for years if you swap the parts that break. Store wooden handles out of the weather and check for cracks; a broken handle mid-cleanup is a common source of cuts and strains.

Backpack sprayers should be cleaned after each use and used only with products labeled for the job, following the label for PPE and mixing. Trimmer line comes in different shapes and diameters; match the size your trimmer head is rated for. Keeping these tools on the truck lets a tree crew finish a job site completely instead of leaving the cleanup for someone else.

faq.q: Is an orchard ladder safe for tree work?
faq.a: Tripod orchard ladders are built for uneven ground, but they still need firm footing, correct setup and use within their rated load. They are not a substitute for climbing gear or an aerial lift on larger trees.

name: Logging Tools
title: Log Tools & Logging Tools for Tree Crews
meta: Log tools and logger tools for tree crews: axes and mauls, cant hooks, hookaroons, log carriers and logging tapes for moving, measuring and splitting wood.
intro: Log tools save backs and speed up cleanup on removals. This section covers the logger tools tree crews use daily: axes and mauls, log handling tools and forestry measuring tapes.

p: A cant hook or peavey rolls logs for bucking and loading, a hookaroon drags and stacks rounds and firewood without bending over, and a log carrier lets two people move heavy rounds. A logging tape on your belt speeds up bucking to length.
An axe or maul splits rounds and drives wedges. Keep edges sharp, handles tight, and inspect tools for cracks before use.

If you buck a lot of logs on the ground, a cant hook will save more strain than any other tool here. If you stack firewood or feed a splitter, a hookaroon is the tool you will reach for most. Crews moving rounds by hand from a backyard to a trailer get the most from a log carrier.

Lighter aluminum handles are easier to carry all day, while wooden handles are cheaper and easy to replace. Keep log tools in a dedicated rack or box on the truck so points and hooks do not get damaged or damage other gear.

faq.q: What is the difference between a cant hook and a peavey?
faq.a: A cant hook has a blunt toe with teeth; a peavey ends in a spike. Both roll logs; the peavey can also pry and pivot.

name: Axes & Mauls
title: Axes and Mauls for Felling, Splitting and Wedging
meta: Axes and mauls for tree crews: universal axes for limbing and driving wedges, splitting axes for rounds, and fiber-handled multi-purpose axes for the truck.
intro: Axes and mauls are basic gear on any removal. A universal axe drives felling wedges and limbs small branches, while a splitting axe or maul opens rounds for firewood.

p: A general-purpose axe with a flat poll is the most useful on a tree crew because it can drive wedges as well as cut. Splitting axes have a wider, wedge-shaped head that pops rounds apart instead of sticking. Fiber handles shrug off weather; hickory handles are traditional and easy to replace.
Keep the edge sharp and covered with a sheath when not in use, and check that the head is tight before each job.

Swing with a clear area around you and your feet set wide. When splitting, place the round on a solid chopping block rather than the ground so a glancing swing hits wood, not your shin. Keep other crew members well outside the swing zone.

Sharpen with a file or stone, keeping the original bevel, and do not grind so hot that the steel loses its temper. Store the axe with its sheath on, and replace a handle that is cracked or loose in the head. A well-kept axe is a tool you will hand down; a neglected one is a hazard.

faq.q: Can I drive felling wedges with any axe?
faq.a: Use an axe with a poll designed for striking. Hitting wedges with an axe not built for it can mushroom or crack the head.

name: Forestry Tools
title: Forestry Supplies: Logging Tapes and Forestry Tools
meta: Forestry supplies and forestry tools for loggers and tree crews: logging tapes with belt clips and refill tapes for measuring and bucking logs to length.
intro: Forestry supplies like logging tapes let you buck to consistent lengths and measure stems without a second person. These forestry tools clip to your belt and are built for rough use.

p: A logging tape has a nail or hook on the end that grabs the log so you can walk the tape out alone. Spring-return housings reel it back in when you finish. Look for a length that covers your typical cuts, and keep a refill tape on hand, because the blade is the part that wears.
Some tapes are marked for diameter on the back so you can measure stems for volume or felling plans. Clip the tape where it will not catch on brush or your saw.

Beyond a logging tape, many crews carry a diameter tape or calipers for measuring trunks, a lumber crayon or spray paint for marking cuts, and a belt or vest to hold it all. These small forestry tools save time when you are bucking logs for a mill, firewood customer or crane pick.

Logging tapes take a beating from mud, sap and sawdust. Rinse and dry the blade now and then, avoid kinking it, and replace the blade when the markings wear off. A refill costs far less than a new tape and housing.

faq.q: Can I replace just the tape in a logging tape?
faq.a: Many logging tapes accept refill blades in matching lengths. Check that the refill fits your housing model.

name: Log Handling
title: Logging Tools: Cant Hooks, Hookaroons & Log Carriers
meta: Logging tools and log handling tools for tree crews: cant hooks, hookaroons and log carriers that roll, drag and lift rounds so you do not have to bend over.
intro: Log handling tools are the logging tools that save your back on every removal. Cant hooks roll stems for bucking, hookaroons grab and drag rounds, and log carriers let two people lift heavy wood without grabbing it by hand.

p: A cant hook uses a swinging hook and a toothed toe to grip and roll a log. On the job it lets you turn a stem so you can finish a cut without hitting dirt, and roll logs onto a trailer or into position for splitting. Aluminum handles are noticeably lighter than wood, which matters when you carry one all day.
Pick a handle length suited to the logs you normally handle: longer handles give more leverage on big stems, shorter ones are handier in tight spots.

To roll a log, set the toe under the log on the side away from you, swing the hook over the top so it bites, and pull the handle toward you. Keep your feet clear of the log's path and roll it a little at a time on slopes. On a crew, two cant hooks on the same log make big stems manageable.

A hookaroon, sometimes called a pickaroon, has a sharp pick on a handle. Swing it into the end grain or side of a round and drag it, stack it or lift it onto a splitter without bending. A long-handled hookaroon gives more reach; a short one is better for firewood and splitting.
Log grabbers and log tongs pinch a round from both sides so you can carry it. They are handy for moving short pieces to the chipper or the truck.

Hookaroons are also handy for pulling brush toward the chipper without reaching near the infeed, though you should never feed a hookaroon into the chipper or hold one near the feed rollers. Keep the pick out of the machine and your hands well back.

A two-person log carrier grabs a round in the middle so two people can carry it at hip height. It is the safest way to move heavy rounds that are too big to toss but not worth bringing in a loader. Walk in step and set loads down together.

Log carriers also work well for lifting rounds onto a log splitter or the tailgate of a truck. Pick one with enough jaw opening for the size of rounds you usually handle, and keep the points sharp so they grip bark and do not slip when the load shifts.

Logging tools keep hands and feet out of pinch points, but they do not change the weight of the wood. Know your limits, lift with your legs, and roll or drag instead of lifting whenever possible. Keep pick points sharp so they bite and do not glance off.

Store log handling tools where the points and hooks cannot hit other gear or people, and replace worn hooks and cracked handles. A tool that slips under load can cause a fall or a crushed hand. Keep a spare hook and bolt kit for your cant hook, since those are the parts that wear first on a busy crew.

faq.q: Do I need a cant hook or a hookaroon?
faq.a: Get a cant hook if you roll logs for bucking or loading. Get a hookaroon if you mostly move rounds and firewood. Many crews carry both.

faq.q: Are aluminum-handled logging tools strong enough?
faq.a: Quality aluminum-handled cant hooks and hookaroons are designed for professional use and are lighter than wood. Use them within the maker's intended purpose and do not use them as pry bars beyond that.

faq.q: What is a log carrier used for?
faq.a: It lets two people lift and carry a round between them without bending over and grabbing it by hand.

faq.q: How do I keep a hookaroon sharp?
faq.a: Touch up the point with a file when it starts glancing off wood, keeping the original shape.

name: Power Equipment
title: Power Equipment: Chainsaws, Blowers, Battery Tools & Parts
meta: Power equipment for arborists and tree crews: pro chainsaws, top-handle saws, battery tools, backpack blowers, trimmers, power cutters and replacement parts.
intro: Power equipment does the heavy lifting on a tree job, from the climbing saw to the backpack blower that cleans up the drive. Browse gas and battery saws, blowers, trimmers and the parts to keep them running.

p: Most crews run a top-handle saw for the climber, a mid-size rear-handle saw for limbing and bucking, and one big saw for removals and stump work. Battery saws are gaining ground for pruning and noise-sensitive jobs. Add a backpack blower for cleanup and stock filters and spark plugs.
Top-handle saws are designed for use in the tree by trained operators only. Read the manual and follow ANSI Z133 for saw use aloft.

Most breakdowns come down to fuel, air and spark. Run fresh or premixed fuel, clean air filters daily in dusty work, and keep spare plugs and fuel filters in the truck. Sharpen chains often, since a dull chain works the engine harder.

Keep a simple log of hours and service for each machine, and send saws to a servicing dealer for carburetor work, chain brake repairs and anything you are unsure about. Train every operator on each machine before they use it, and never remove factory safety features.

faq.q: Should I switch to battery-powered equipment?
faq.a: Battery saws and blowers work well for pruning, small removals and residential cleanup. Most crews still keep gas saws for heavy wood.

name: Battery Equipment
title: Battery-Powered Chainsaws, Blowers & Chargers
meta: Battery-powered chainsaw options for arborists: top-handle battery saws, rear-handle saws, handheld blowers and quick chargers for quieter tree work.
intro: A battery-powered chainsaw starts instantly, runs quiet and has no fuel to mix, which makes it a strong choice for pruning and residential work. Pair the saws with a handheld blower and a fast charger to keep batteries cycling all day.

guide.h: Running battery gear on a crew
p: Plan on enough batteries to rotate: one in the tool, one on the charger and a spare. A quick charger and a vehicle inverter or generator keep that cycle going. Battery top-handle saws are popular with climbers because there is no pull start in the tree and less noise for talking to the ground crew.
Battery tools still cut like any saw, so the same PPE, training and ANSI Z133 practices apply. Store batteries in moderate temperatures and follow the maker's charging guidance.

Battery top-handle saws are excellent for pruning, deadwooding and small removals, and their quiet operation helps on residential and early morning jobs. A battery rear-handle saw handles limbing and smaller bucking. For heavy hardwood and big diameter cuts, most crews still reach for gas.

Keep batteries out of extreme heat and cold, carry them in a case, and do not charge a hot battery until it cools. Batteries are expensive, so treat them like any other key tool. Chain sharpness matters even more on battery saws, since a dull chain drains runtime fast.

faq.q: How long does a battery chainsaw run?
faq.a: It depends on the battery size and how hard you cut. Pruning goes much further than bucking hardwood, so carry spares for a full day.

name: Blowers & Trimmers
h1: Backpack Blowers, Trimmers and Power Cutters
title: Backpack Blowers, String Trimmers & Power Cutters
meta: Backpack blower picks for tree crew cleanup, plus handheld blowers, string trimmers, combi-tool trimmers and power cutters for site and grounds work.
intro: A strong backpack blower is the fastest way to leave a job site cleaner than you found it. This section also covers handheld blowers, string trimmers and power cutters for crews that handle more than trees.

p: Backpack blowers move sawdust and chips off driveways and lawns quickly and are easier on the arms than handheld models for long cleanups. Handheld blowers are fine for small jobs and quick touch-ups. String trimmers and combination tools handle edges and growth around stumps.
Power cutters are for concrete, steel and masonry, not wood. Wear eye and hearing protection with all of this gear, and keep bystanders clear of blower debris.

Clean the air filter often, especially in sawdust-heavy cleanups. Check that intake guards and screens are in place so debris cannot be pulled into the fan. For trimmers, keep the head clean and use line in the diameter the head is designed for.

Power cutters need the right wheel for the material, and the wheel must be rated for the cutter's speed. Store fuel-powered equipment with fresh or stabilized fuel, or run it dry for long storage. Hearing and eye protection are a must with all of these tools.

faq.q: Do I need a backpack blower or a handheld?
faq.a: For daily crew cleanup a backpack blower saves time and fatigue. A handheld is a good second unit for quick jobs.

name: Chainsaws
title: Arborist Chainsaws: Top-Handle, Pro & Felling Saws
meta: Arborist chainsaw lineup for tree crews: top-handle climbing saws, mid-size pro saws for limbing and bucking, big felling saws and a gas pole saw for pruning.
intro: The right arborist chainsaw depends on where it runs: in the tree, on the ground or in the big wood. These saws cover top-handle climbing saws, mid-size professional saws, large felling saws and a pole saw.

guide.h: Matching the saw to the job
p: Top-handle saws are light and compact for one-handed control aloft, and are meant only for trained operators working in the tree. Mid-size rear-handle saws are the workhorses for limbing, bucking and smaller removals. Large saws in the 70 cc and up class pull long bars through big trunks and stumps.
A gas pole saw reaches limbs from the ground for clearance pruning. Whatever the saw, check the chain brake, chain catcher and throttle lockout daily and wear full PPE.

Run fresh, properly mixed fuel or premix, keep air filters clean, and sharpen chain often. A saw that is hard to start or bogs under load usually needs a clean filter or fresh fuel before anything else. For deeper issues, take it to a servicing dealer.

Pick bar length to match the work, not the biggest bar the saw will pull. A shorter bar is lighter, easier to control and less prone to kickback. ANSI Z133 sets requirements for chainsaw use in tree work, including starting procedures and PPE; follow it and the owner's manual. Training is the most important accessory any saw can have.

faq.q: What chainsaw do most arborists climb with?
faq.a: Most climbers use a gas or battery top-handle saw with a short bar. Use top-handle saws only in the tree and only with proper training.

name: Parts
h1: Chainsaw Parts and Power Equipment Parts
title: Chainsaw Parts: Spark Plugs, Fuel Filters & Kits
meta: Chainsaw parts that keep pro saws running: spark plugs, fuel filters, maintenance kits for popular models and a diamond cutting wheel for power cutters.
intro: Common chainsaw parts like spark plugs and fuel filters are cheap and quick to change, and keeping a few on the truck avoids losing half a day to a saw that will not start.

p: Spark plugs, fuel filters and air filters are the parts that wear first. Match the plug to the type listed in the owner's manual; the wrong heat range or reach can damage the engine. Maintenance kits bundle the common wear items for a specific saw model.
Swap fuel filters at least once a season and any time the saw bogs under load. For anything beyond routine wear parts, take the saw to a servicing dealer.
Keep a small bin on the truck with plugs, fuel filters, air filters, a starter rope and a couple of bar nuts for each model your crew runs. Label it by saw model so anyone can grab the right part.

Gap the spark plug as listed in the manual if it is not pre-gapped, and torque it to spec. A fresh plug and fuel filter fix more no-start problems than most people expect. Diamond wheels for power cutters are matched to material and cutter size; check both before ordering.

faq.q: How do I find the right spark plug?
faq.a: Use the plug type listed in your owner's manual or the one installed from the factory.

name: Stump Grinding
h1: Stump Grinding Teeth and Stump Grinder Parts
title: Stump Grinding Teeth & Stump Grinder Parts
meta: Stump grinding teeth and stump grinder parts: replacement pocket teeth, bolt-on teeth and standard teeth for faster grinding, plus tips on rotation and safety.
intro: Sharp stump grinding teeth are the difference between a stump that disappears and one that drags on all afternoon. We carry replacement teeth and stump grinder parts for common wheel systems.

p: Most grinders use one of a few tooth systems. Standard bolt-on teeth mount in pairs with a pocket or holder on each side of the wheel. Pocket-style systems hold a tooth in a pocket that bolts to the wheel. Some systems use an Allen-head bolt. Each system needs its own teeth, pockets and hardware, so match the system already on your wheel.

Carbide-tipped teeth hold an edge much longer than plain steel, but carbide chips if it hits rock or metal. That is why checking a stump for buried stones, wire and nails before you start is worth the time.

Stump grinder teeth wear unevenly across a wheel. The outer teeth that do most of the cutting on the sweep wear faster than inner ones. Many operators move teeth around the wheel at rotation time to spread wear and get more life out of a set.

Many teeth can be rotated to present a fresh edge before they need replacing. Rotate when grinding slows or the machine starts working harder. Replace teeth that are chipped, cracked or worn to the shank, and replace bolts and nuts when they are stretched or damaged.
Torque hardware to the manufacturer's spec and replace teeth in balanced sets so the wheel stays balanced. An unbalanced wheel shakes the machine and wears bearings.

Keep spare teeth, pockets, bolts and nuts in a labeled box on the truck along with the correct wrenches and a torque wrench. A broken tooth halfway through a job is a quick fix if you have the parts and a ten-minute delay if you do not. Clean the wheel and pockets before installing new teeth so they seat properly.

Grinders throw chips and stones with real force. Keep the stump grinder guard and shields in place and in good shape, and replace a torn shield promptly. A ground protection mat or a portable debris screen around the stump also keeps chips off windows and cars.

Stump grinder shields and guards are wear parts too. Rubber and composite shields get chewed by debris over time and lose their effectiveness. Check them as part of your daily walkaround and order replacements before the old ones tear through, so you are never tempted to run without them on a job.

Call before you dig to locate underground utilities, keep bystanders well back, wear eye, face and hearing protection, and follow the machine manufacturer's instructions. Never reach toward the wheel until it has fully stopped.

Before grinding, clear the area of rocks and debris, mark irrigation lines and plan where the chips will go. After grinding, rake out the hole, check for any roots near the surface and backfill if the customer wants the area ready for planting.

faq.q: How long do stump grinder teeth last?
faq.a: It depends on soil, rocks and wood type. Teeth in sandy or rocky ground wear much faster. Check them every stump on a big job.

faq.q: Can I mix tooth brands on one wheel?
faq.a: Only if they are made for the same tooth system and pocket. Mixing systems can cause poor fit and unsafe operation.

faq.q: Do I need to replace teeth in sets?
faq.a: Replacing in balanced sets helps keep the wheel balanced and cutting evenly.

faq.q: Why is my stump grinder vibrating?
faq.a: Worn, missing or mismatched teeth are common causes. Stop, lock out the machine and inspect the wheel and hardware.

name: Plant Care
h1: Tree Care Supplies for Plant Health Work
title: Tree Care Supplies: Cabling, Bracing & Planting
meta: Tree care supplies for plant health work: tree cabling and bracing hardware, planting and staking supplies and wound treatment for the arborist's service truck.
intro: Tree care supplies cover the work that keeps trees standing and healthy: cabling and bracing systems, planting and staking hardware, and wound treatment. This department is for arborists who offer more than removals.

p: Supplemental support systems reduce the risk of failure in weak unions and heavy limbs. Steel cable systems use EHS or common grade cable with eye bolts or lags, while bracing rods add rigid support across a split or weak crotch. Installation should follow ANSI A300 support system standards and be done by trained arborists.
Plan for inspection. A support system is not install-and-forget; it should be checked on a schedule and adjusted or replaced as the tree grows.

Common cabling hardware includes eye bolts, eye lag screws and J-lags. Eye bolts through the limb give the strongest anchor; lag hardware threads into the wood and suits lighter systems. The right choice depends on limb size, wood condition and the loads the system is expected to handle.

Newly planted trees sometimes need temporary staking to stay upright until roots establish. Wide, soft tree straps spread load on the bark, and earth anchors hold guys in place without driving stakes through the root ball. Remove staking once the tree can stand on its own, usually within the first year or so.
Plant at the right depth with the root flare visible, mulch wide and shallow, and keep mulch off the trunk.

Good planting supplies make staking easy to do right. Tree support webbing comes on a roll so you can cut what you need, and duck bill style earth anchors drive in with a rod and set by pulling up. Wire rope clamps finish guy lines to anchors when installed as the clamp maker specifies. Check staked trees during the season to make sure straps are not rubbing or cutting into the bark.

Most pruning cuts heal best when made correctly and left alone. Some arborists use wound treatment on specific species or in specific situations, such as reducing pest attraction. Follow local guidance and the product label.

Wound treatment is not a substitute for good pruning. Make cuts just outside the branch collar, avoid flush cuts and leave the tree's natural defenses intact. If a wound needs attention for disease or pest reasons, follow local extension or certified arborist guidance.

Plant health care is a skilled service. If you are a homeowner, we suggest hiring an ISA-certified arborist to assess and install support systems. If you are a pro, use the supplies here alongside current standards and your own training.

Our goal with this department is to keep the common consumables in one place so a plant health crew can restock quickly. Pair these supplies with good record keeping: note what was installed or applied, where and when, so follow-up visits are efficient and the customer understands the value of ongoing care.

faq.q: What standard covers tree cabling and bracing?
faq.a: In the US, ANSI A300 includes a part on supplemental support systems. Follow it along with your company's procedures.

faq.q: How long should a newly planted tree stay staked?
faq.a: Only as long as needed, often one growing season. Long-term staking can weaken the trunk.

faq.q: Is pruning sealer necessary?
faq.a: Usually not. A correct cut is the main thing; some situations call for treatment, so follow local guidance.

faq.q: Can a homeowner install a tree cabling kit?
faq.a: We recommend hiring a qualified arborist. Cabling involves working at height and judging tree structure.

name: Cabling & Bracing
title: Tree Cable, Cabling Kits & Bracing Supplies
meta: Tree cable and tree cabling supplies for arborists: EHS and common grade cable, bracing rods and hardware to build tree cabling kits and bracing systems.
intro: Tree cable and bracing rods are the backbone of supplemental support systems. Use these tree cabling supplies to build a tree cabling kit for the service truck or to restock after a job.

p: Extra high strength (EHS) galvanized cable is the common choice for most tree support work because it offers high strength for its diameter. Common grade cable is lower strength and suits lighter applications. The right size depends on the diameter of the limbs being supported and the system design, so size by the standard and your company's specs rather than by guesswork.
Cable is usually installed with eye bolts or lag hardware and terminated with preformed dead-ends or other approved terminations. Do not mix incompatible hardware and cable sizes.

Static steel systems are the traditional choice for heavy limbs and codominant stems. Common grade cable can work for smaller trees or lighter loads. Do not substitute hardware store wire or cable not meant for this use, since it may not have the strength or corrosion resistance needed.

Threaded bracing rods give rigid support across a split or a weak union where movement must be limited. They are installed through the stem with washers and nuts. Bracing is often used together with cabling higher in the crown.

Bracing rods are typically installed in pairs or sets through the stems near a weak union, with washers sized to spread load on the wood. Proper drilling and placement matter, and holes should be no larger than needed. A bracing kit can include rods, nuts, washers and a drill bit sized for the rod.

Not every split or weak union is a good candidate for bracing. Decay, cracks running deep into the stem or a target-rich site may call for reduction, removal or a different approach. A risk assessment by a qualified arborist should come before any hardware goes into the tree.

A practical kit includes a few sizes of cable, matching eye bolts and lags, terminations, thimbles, a drill with long bits, a cable cutter and a way to measure and tension. Keep hardware sorted by size so the climber gets what they ask for the first time.
Some crews also carry synthetic dynamic systems for lighter support. Those use their own hardware and installation methods.

Keep a written checklist in the kit and restock after each install. Running short on a single eye bolt size halfway up a tree costs more time than it saves. Label sizes clearly on bins and bags, and carry a few extra of the most common parts.

Install support systems according to ANSI A300 and the manufacturer's instructions. Document what was installed and schedule follow-up inspections, since trees grow and hardware ages. Tree bracing systems that are not inspected can become part of the problem.

Tree cabling supplies should be stored dry and free of corrosion. Discard bent or damaged hardware rather than straightening it. When installing in a customer's tree, explain that the system needs periodic inspection, and put the next inspection date on the invoice.

faq.q: What is the difference between EHS and common grade cable?
faq.a: EHS cable has a much higher breaking strength for the same diameter. It is the usual choice for tree support systems.

faq.q: Can I use guy wire for tree cabling?
faq.a: Guy wire for planting is a different application. Use cable and hardware intended for tree support systems.

faq.q: How often should a cabled tree be inspected?
faq.a: Follow the system designer's recommendations, commonly at regular intervals and after major storms.

faq.q: Do I need special training to install tree cabling?
faq.a: Yes. Installation involves climbing or aerial work and structural judgment, and should follow ANSI A300.

name: Cabling Hardware
title: Tree Cabling Hardware: Eye Bolts & Lag Screws
meta: Tree cabling hardware for support systems: galvanized eye bolts, eye lag screws and J-lags to anchor cable in limbs, plus notes on guy wires for trees.
intro: Tree cabling hardware anchors the cable to the tree. Eye bolts go through the limb for the strongest hold, while eye lags and J-lags thread into the wood for lighter loads or where through-bolting is not practical.

p: Through-bolted eye bolts with washers and nuts are the strongest anchor and are used for larger limbs and higher loads. Lag-type anchors are faster to install and suit smaller limbs. Match the hardware size to the cable and follow ANSI A300 guidance on placement and hole size.
Galvanized hardware resists corrosion. For guy wires for trees during planting, use soft straps and earth anchors rather than hardware driven into the trunk.

Drill holes to the size the hardware maker and ANSI A300 call for, and place anchors in sound wood, avoiding decay and cracks. Align the anchor with the cable so it pulls straight rather than bending the shank. Use the same metal type across the system to avoid corrosion where parts touch.

Record the hardware type, size and location for each tree. That makes follow-up inspections faster and lets the next arborist understand the system. Galvanized eye lag screws and J-lags are handy for small, lighter systems; through-bolted eye bolts are the go-to on bigger limbs and higher loads.

faq.q: Should I use an eye bolt or eye lag?
faq.a: Eye bolts through the limb hold more and are preferred on larger limbs. Lags are for smaller limbs and lighter systems.

name: Planting
title: Tree Planting Supplies: Straps, Anchors & Clamps
meta: Tree planting supplies for staking and guying new trees: soft tree support webbing, duck bill earth anchors and wire rope clamps for a clean, secure install.
intro: Tree planting supplies help new trees stay upright while the roots take hold. Soft webbing protects bark, earth anchors hold guys without stakes, and wire rope clamps secure the line.

p: Use the least support that keeps the tree upright, and attach low enough that the trunk can still flex. Wide webbing spreads load and will not girdle the bark like bare wire. Duck bill earth anchors drive into the soil and lock when pulled, which is faster than driving wooden stakes.
Check staking a few times during the season and remove it once the tree can stand on its own, often after one growing season.

guide.h: Planting tips that help trees establish
p: Dig the hole wide and no deeper than the root ball, with the root flare at or slightly above grade. Remove wire baskets and burlap from the top of the ball as local guidance recommends, and correct circling roots. Water deeply and regularly during the first season.

When guying, attach to the trunk with soft, wide material and use earth anchors set outside the root ball. Wire rope clamps secure guy cable to anchors; install them as the clamp maker specifies. Check the setup after storms, and plan the date you will remove staking when you install it.

faq.q: How tight should tree staking be?
faq.a: Snug enough to keep the tree upright but loose enough to let the trunk move a bit, which helps it build strength.

name: Rigging
title: Arborist Rigging: Slings, Blocks & Lowering Devices
meta: Arborist rigging equipment for removals and pruning: rigging slings, blocks and pulleys, lowering devices, mechanical advantage systems and rigging kits.
intro: Arborist rigging is how crews take trees apart piece by piece without dropping wood on roofs, fences and lawns. This department covers rigging slings, blocks and pulleys, lowering devices, mechanical advantage systems and ready-made rigging kits.

guide.h: How a rigging system fits together
p: A basic system has an anchor point in the tree, a rigging block or pulley hung on a sling, a rigging rope running through it, and a friction device on the ground to control the load. The climber ties or slings the piece being cut, makes the cut, and the ground worker lets it run and stops it under control.

Every part has a rated strength, and the weakest component sets the limit. Rigging loads are dynamic: a piece that drops even a short distance before the rope catches it can generate forces several times its weight. Plan cuts to keep drops short.

A tree rigging setup should be planned from the ground before anyone climbs. Decide where pieces will land, where the block will hang, how the rope will run and where the ground worker will stand. Talk the plan through with the crew and agree on commands.

Arborist slings attach blocks and pulleys to the tree and choke the pieces being lowered. Eye-to-eye slings, whoopie slings that adjust in length, round slings for cranes and heavy dead-eye slings each have a place. Rigging rings and steel hardware add options for redirects and friction setups.

Choose slings rated at least as high as the blocks and rope they work with. Protect slings from the saw and sharp edges, and do not use any sling with an unknown rating. Rigging rings are useful for building friction redirects and anchors, but they need to be rated for the loads they will see.

A lowering device such as a Port-a-Wrap or a bollard-style tool mounts on the trunk or a sling and puts controlled friction on the rigging line. Mechanical advantage systems help pull trees over, tension lines and lift loads. Speed line kits move brush across a yard to the drop zone on a tensioned line.

The rigging rope ties it all together. It should be sized to the loads you plan to lower and matched to the blocks and lowering devices in the system. Rigging rope and climbing rope must stay separate; a climbing line should never be used for rigging, and rigging rope is never used for climbing.

Rigging gear is not life support, but a failure can still hurt people. Use gear within its working load, inspect slings and rope before every job, retire damaged gear, and follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions. Rigging is learned best with a qualified trainer and hands-on practice.

If you are building a rigging kit from scratch, start small and add pieces as you learn. Many crews begin with a rigging rope, a block, a few slings and a lowering device, then add mechanical advantage and speed lines as their removals get bigger.

faq.q: What rigging gear does a small tree crew need first?
faq.a: A rigging rope, a rigging block, a couple of slings, a lowering device and carabiners or shackles rated for rigging. Add mechanical advantage and speed line gear as your jobs grow.

faq.q: How strong does arborist rigging gear need to be?
faq.a: Strong enough for dynamic loads with a margin. Know the working load of each component and plan cuts to keep shock loading low.

faq.q: Can climbing carabiners be used for rigging?
faq.a: Use hardware rated and intended for rigging loads. Keep life-support gear separate from rigging gear.

faq.q: How do I learn to rig safely?
faq.a: Train with a qualified instructor, practice on low-consequence pieces and follow ANSI Z133 and your company's procedures.

name: Blocks & Hardware
title: Rigging Block, Arborist Pulleys & Rigging Hardware
meta: Rigging block, arborist pulley and rigging hardware options: steel and aluminum blocks, swing-cheek pulleys, rigging plates, rings, clevises and hooks.
intro: A rigging block redirects the rigging rope in the tree and takes the load when a piece is lowered. This section groups arborist blocks, pulleys, rigging plates and steel hardware.

p: Arborist blocks are built for the high, dynamic loads of lowering wood and are sized by rope diameter. Smaller pulleys handle lighter rigging, redirects and mechanical advantage systems. A rigging plate creates multiple attachment points at an anchor for organized setups.
Check the rated strength, rope size and sheave diameter, and pair blocks with slings rated for the same loads. Inspect sheaves for wear and side plates for damage before use.

Start from your rope diameter and the biggest pieces you expect to lower. That sets the block size, and the block sets the sling and connectors. Swing-side pulleys open to load the rope mid-line, which saves time on redirects and speed lines. Steel hardware such as rings and clevises builds friction setups, redirects and pulling systems.

Every component carries a rated strength. In rigging the weakest link sets the system's limit, and dynamic loading can multiply forces. Keep rigging hardware separate from climbing hardware, and retire anything that is bent, cracked or shows sheave wear.

faq.q: What is the difference between a rigging block and a pulley?
faq.a: Blocks are generally heavier and built for big dynamic rigging loads. Pulleys are lighter and used for smaller loads, redirects and haul systems.

name: Rigging Blocks
title: Rigging Block Options: Arborist Blocks for 5/8 Rope
meta: Rigging block choices for tree removals: steel arborist blocks and compact rigging pulleys sized for up to 5/8 inch rope, with tips on slings and loads.
intro: A rigging block hangs from a sling high in the tree and carries the rigging rope while pieces are lowered. These arborist blocks are sized for common rigging rope diameters.

p: Match the block to your rope diameter and to the loads you expect. A steel block is heavy but tough enough for big removals; smaller aluminum blocks suit lighter rigging. The sling attaching the block should be rated at least as high as the block.

Remember that the load on the block can be nearly double the load on the rope when the line runs back down, and more under shock loading. Keep drops short and inspect the sheave and side plates often.

Hang the block on a rated sling wrapped around solid wood above the piece being cut, and keep it close to the trunk to reduce leverage on the stem. Make sure the rope runs cleanly through the sheave without rubbing the side plates or sling.

Arborist block and tackle setups add mechanical advantage for lifting or tensioning, but they also multiply force on the anchor. Check sheave bearings or bushings for smooth spin, side plates for bends, and the attachment point for wear. Retire any block that has been overloaded or dropped from height onto hard ground.

faq.q: What size rigging block do I need?
faq.a: Size it to your rigging rope diameter and the heaviest pieces you plan to lower, with a good margin for dynamic loading.

name: Rigging Pulleys
h1: Tree Pulley and Arborist Rigging Pulleys
title: Tree Pulley Options: Arborist Rigging Pulleys
meta: Tree pulley and arborist rigging pulley options: swing-side pulleys, double pulleys and a downrigger for light rigging, redirects and haul systems in tree work.
intro: A tree pulley redirects rope for light rigging, speed lines and mechanical advantage systems. Rigging pulleys are lighter than blocks and quicker to set.

p: Swing-side pulleys open to load the rope mid-line, which saves time. Double pulleys build compact haul systems. A downrigger mounts on the trunk to add friction and control for lowering lines from aloft.
Check rated strength and maximum rope diameter for each pulley, and never use a light rescue or haul pulley for heavy, dynamic rigging loads.

Larger sheave diameters bend the rope less and keep more of its strength. Pulleys with bearings run more freely than bushings, which matters in haul systems where friction adds up. Double pulleys make 3:1 and 5:1 systems more compact.

Clip pulleys to anchors with rated connectors and slings, and set them so the rope runs cleanly without rubbing side plates. Keep life-support pulleys separate from rigging pulleys, and inspect sheaves for grooves and side plates for bends. Retire a pulley that has been overloaded or dropped.

faq.q: Can I use a climbing pulley for rigging?
faq.a: Only within its rated load, and keep life-support pulleys separate from rigging gear.

name: Rings & Hardware
h1: Rigging Hardware: Clevises, Hooks and Connectors
title: Rigging Hardware: Clevises, Chain Hooks & Connectors
meta: Rigging hardware for tree crews: galvanized clevises, chain choker hooks and chain connectors for pulling, skidding and connecting rigging components.
intro: Rigging hardware like clevises, hooks and chain connectors joins chain, slings and rope when pulling, skidding or anchoring loads. Use rated hardware sized to the job.

p: A galvanized clevis connects a chain or sling to a hitch or anchor. Chain choker hooks let you choke a log with chain and release it quickly. Chain connectors join chain sections or attach fittings.
Check the working load limit marked on each piece, use pins that match, and retire hardware that is bent, cracked or worn. Do not use rigging hardware as life support.

guide.h: Where tree crews use steel hardware
p: Chain chokers with hooks are common for skidding logs, pulling stumps and handling big wood with a loader or truck. Clevises attach chains and slings to tow points and anchors. Rigging rings create low-friction redirects and anchors, and help build adjustable friction setups.

Look for forged, rated hardware with the working load limit marked. Do not side-load hooks or clevises in ways they are not designed for, and do not swap pins between different pieces. Store steel hardware dry and away from synthetic slings so sharp edges and rust do not damage them.

faq.q: Is a clevis rated for overhead lifting?
faq.a: Only if it is marked and rated for that use. Check the manufacturer's markings and working load limit.

name: Lowering Devices
title: Lowering Device Options: Port-a-Wraps & Lowering Gear
meta: Lowering device options for tree rigging: Port-a-Wraps, bollard-style lowering gear and control systems that add friction to rigging lines on the ground.
intro: A lowering device puts controlled friction on the rigging rope so the ground worker can let a piece run and stop it smoothly. This lowering gear mounts on the trunk or a sling.

p: Port-a-Wrap style devices are simple and light: wrap the rope a set number of times to adjust friction. Larger devices handle bigger rope and heavier pieces. Bollard-style systems with a winch or locking feature let one person lower, hold and even lift loads.
Size the device to your rope and loads, attach it to the tree with a rated sling, and keep hands clear of the wraps. Train on smaller pieces before running heavy wood.

Mount the lowering device on the trunk or a sound anchor near the base of the tree, in line with the rigging line's direction. Place it where the ground worker has a clear view of the piece and a safe spot to stand outside the drop zone.

Lowering gear sees a lot of heat and rope wear. Check the horns or bollard for grooves, check the mounting sling and connector, and keep the device clean of grit. Some systems, like those with a winch or ratchet, also let you lift or tension, which helps with pull lines and speed lines. Learn each device's limits from the manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: How many wraps should I use on a Port-a-Wrap?
faq.a: It depends on the load, rope and device. Start with more friction than you think you need and follow the manufacturer's guidance.

name: Mechanical Advantage
title: Mechanical Advantage System Gear & Rope Pullers
meta: Mechanical advantage systems for arborists: continuous rope pullers, tree pulling kits and progress-capture pulleys for tensioning lines and pulling trees.
intro: Mechanical advantage systems let a crew pull trees over, tension speed lines and lift loads with less effort. Options here include continuous rope pullers and progress-capture pulleys for a tree pulling kit.

p: A continuous rope puller grips the rope as you ratchet the handle, so you can pull long distances without re-rigging. A progress-capture pulley holds the rope between pulls, which makes a simple 3:1 or 5:1 pulley system practical.
Remember that more advantage means more force on the anchor and the tree. Use rated anchors, keep people out of the line of fire, and plan the fall before you start pulling.

For pulling trees, many crews use a continuous rope puller or a simple pulley system with a progress-capture device. Rope pullers are fast to set and pull long distances, while pulley systems are light and use gear you already carry. A good tree pulling kit includes a rated anchor sling, the puller or pulleys, connectors and enough rope.

Mechanical prusik setups and progress capture devices hold tension between pulls. Keep everyone out of the line of fire if a component fails, and never pull more than the anchor and tree can handle. Train on setups at low loads before using them on a job.

faq.q: What is a 5 to 1 pulley system used for?
faq.a: Arborists use it to pull trees in a chosen direction or tension lines. It multiplies pulling force but also loads anchors heavily.

name: Rigging Kits
title: Arborist Rigging Kit Options: Speed Lines & Port-a-Wrap
meta: Arborist rigging kit options for tree crews: speed line kits with carabiners and Port-a-Wrap with sling kits that bundle matched gear for common rigging jobs.
intro: An arborist rigging kit bundles matched components so you can set up a common system without hunting for parts. These rigging kits cover speed lines and a lowering setup with a sling.

p: A speed line runs from high in the tree to an anchor on the ground. Brush and small wood clipped to the line slides down to the drop zone instead of landing on lawns and gardens. Kits typically include a pulley or trolley, carabiners or snaps and the hardware to tension the line.
Set the line steep enough for loads to slide, tension it with mechanical advantage, and keep people clear of the line and landing area. A tag line helps control loads near the bottom.

Speed lines are especially useful when the drop zone is far from the tree or blocked by structures, gardens or fences. They reduce the number of trips the ground crew makes dragging brush and keep turf damage down. Plan the line's path so it clears obstacles and lands loads where the ground crew can unclip them safely.

A Port-a-Wrap with a soft anchor rigging sling gives you a ready-to-go friction device to mount on the trunk. It is a good first lowering setup for small crews and pairs with any rigging rope in its size range.

A soft anchor sling wraps around the trunk and gives the lowering device a secure mount without hardware that could damage bark. Choose the sling length to fit the trees you usually work on, and make sure the device sits in line with the rigging rope's direction of pull.

A Port-a-Wrap kit is also handy as a second lowering point on bigger removals, or for controlling a pull line or tag line. Inspect the device for grooves worn by rope, check that the sling is free of cuts and abrasion, and store the kit together so nothing goes missing between jobs.

Kits remove guesswork about compatibility. The parts are sized to work together and to similar strengths. You can still add or swap components later as your rigging grows, but starting with a matched kit avoids weak links.
Check the rated strength of every component, including carabiners and slings, and inspect the kit before each use. Kits are for rigging loads, not life support.

If you already own some components, check whether a kit duplicates them. Sometimes buying the missing pieces separately is cheaper. When in doubt, compare the rated strength, rope diameter range and connector type of every piece so the final system has no weak spots.
Rigging setups are simple to buy and easy to get wrong. Learn from a qualified trainer, follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions, and practice on light loads first.

Rope compatibility is another reason to train first. Each friction device and pulley in a kit works best with a certain rope diameter range. Using the wrong rope can make a device grab too much or too little. Read the instructions included with each component before the first job.

faq.q: What comes in an arborist rigging kit?
faq.a: It depends on the kit. Speed line kits usually include a pulley and carabiners; lowering kits include a friction device and sling.

faq.q: Can rigging kit carabiners be used for climbing?
faq.a: Keep rigging and life-support gear separate. Use climbing connectors only for climbing.

faq.q: How do I tension a speed line?
faq.a: Most crews use a mechanical advantage system or a friction device to tension the line, keeping within the rated strength of the components.

faq.q: Is a rigging kit good for a beginner?
faq.a: A kit is a good starting point, but rigging requires training and supervised practice.

name: Rigging Slings
title: Rigging Sling Options: Arborist Slings & Runners
meta: Rigging sling options for arborists: heavy-duty webbing slings, loop runners, whoopie slings, crane round slings and dead-eye rigging slings for tree work.
intro: A rigging sling attaches blocks and pulleys to the tree and chokes the pieces being lowered. This collection of arborist slings covers webbing, rope and round slings.

p: Webbing slings and loop runners are flat and grip bark well for anchoring blocks. Rope slings such as dead-eye slings choke wood and pass easily through crotches. Adjustable whoopie slings change length quickly to fit different stem sizes. Round slings are used for crane picks.
Pick slings rated for your heaviest loads, protect them from saw cuts and sharp edges, and retire any sling that is cut, burned, abraded or has a missing tag.

Slings work hard and often sit right next to the cut, so keep the saw clear and protect slings at sharp edges. Rotate where you choke a sling so wear spreads out, and wash them now and then to remove grit that cuts fibers from the inside.

Retire any sling that is cut, melted, heavily abraded, stiff, or has damaged splices or stitching, and any sling whose tag or rating is unknown. Rigging rings combined with slings create friction setups and redirects; use rings rated for rigging loads. Keep a few sizes and types so you can match the sling to the job.

faq.q: How do I choose a sling length?
faq.a: It should wrap the stem with room to choke or basket it. Adjustable slings cover a range of sizes.

name: Adjustable Slings
h1: Adjustable Slings: Whoopie Slings for Rigging
title: Adjustable Sling Options: Whoopie Slings for Rigging
meta: Adjustable sling options for tree rigging: whoopie slings in 1/2, 3/4 and 5/8 inch sizes that change length fast to anchor blocks and choke wood.
intro: An adjustable sling, usually a whoopie sling, lets you set the length in seconds so one sling fits many stem sizes. Arborists use them to hang blocks and choke pieces.

p: A whoopie sling has a fixed eye on one end and a buried, adjustable section that locks under load. Pull it snug around the stem and the bury grips. Use the size and strength suited to the load and the block.
Do not adjust a whoopie under load, keep the adjustable section within its marked range, and inspect the bury and eyes for wear before every job.
