Smaller diameters, such as 1/2 inch, suit light rigging and redirects. Larger sizes such as 5/8 and 3/4 inch handle heavier wood and hold blocks for bigger removals. Pick the size that matches your block and loads, and carry a couple so you can set one for the block and another for the piece.

Whoopies are also handy for friction devices mounted on the trunk and for anchoring speed lines. Keep them clean and away from the saw, and retire any sling that shows a cut, heavy glazing or a damaged bury.

faq.q: Can a whoopie sling slip?
faq.a: When used within its range and loaded correctly it locks. Damaged or overextended slings can fail, so inspect them.

name: Crane Slings
title: Crane Slings & Tree Slings for Crane Removals
meta: Crane slings and tree slings for crane-assisted removals: endless round slings and premium rope crane slings with tags, plus tips on hitches and inspection.
intro: Crane slings attach a tree section to the crane hook, so they carry the whole pick. For crane-assisted tree removal, we stock endless round slings and premium rope tree slings built for heavy, controlled lifts.

p: Endless polyester round slings have a load-bearing core inside a protective cover. They are soft on bark, grip well in a choker hitch and are color-coded by rated capacity on many products. Rope crane slings with spliced eyes are durable and easy to set on rough stems.
Whichever you choose, the sling's tag shows its rated capacity in vertical, choker and basket hitches. A sling without a readable tag should not be used for crane work.

A tree sling for crane work should be long enough to wrap the stem with room to spare and to reach the hook comfortably. Many crews carry several lengths and capacities so they can match the sling to each pick. Round slings fold small for storage, which helps on trucks that are already full.

Round slings and rope slings each have a learning curve. Round slings can roll on smooth stems, so set them with a choke that bites, and rope slings can be stiffer to set on small stems. Try both on lower-stakes picks to learn how they behave before a big job.

A choker hitch reduces a sling's rated capacity compared to a vertical lift, and a basket hitch can increase it, depending on angles. Sling angles matter: the flatter the angle, the more load on each leg. Work with the crane operator and the lift plan so the pick stays inside the rated capacity of every component.

Crane straps and crane slings should be rated with margin above the expected weight of the pick. Tree sections are hard to estimate, and green wood is heavier than people think. Work from weight charts for the species and diameter where possible, and use the crane's load indicator to confirm before cutting free.

Saw chain, sharp stubs and rough bark can cut a sling. Set slings away from the cut, use sleeves or protection where they pass over edges, and cut well clear of the sling. Store slings clean, dry and out of sunlight.

Never let a sling get pinched in the kerf or cut by the climber's saw. Place slings with enough distance above the cut so the saw stays well clear. Some crews use protective sleeves on slings where they cross rough bark or edges.

Inspect crane slings before each shift for cuts, burns, broken stitches, exposed core and chemical damage, and remove damaged slings from service. Crane-assisted tree work should follow ANSI Z133, the crane manufacturer's instructions and applicable crane rules, and involve qualified riggers and operators.

Crane slinging is a specialized skill. Climbers and ground crew working with cranes should be trained in crane signals, rigging and the specific hazards of crane-assisted removals. Keep a clear exclusion zone under the load and follow the lift plan.

faq.q: What is the best sling for crane tree removal?
faq.a: Many crews use endless round slings or rope crane slings rated well above the expected pick. The right choice depends on the lift plan.

faq.q: Does a choker hitch reduce sling capacity?
faq.a: Yes. Check the sling tag for its choker rating and plan around that number.

faq.q: Can I use an arborist sling for a crane pick?
faq.a: Only if it is rated and tagged for that load and hitch. Most crane work calls for slings made and tagged for lifting.

faq.q: When should I retire a crane sling?
faq.a: Retire it if it is cut, burned, has exposed core yarns, broken stitching, a missing tag or any damage the manufacturer lists.

name: Heavy-Duty Slings
h1: Heavy Duty Slings for Tree Rigging
title: Heavy Duty Sling Options: Dead-Eye & Bull Rope Slings
meta: Heavy duty sling options for big rigging: dead-eye slings, bull rope rigging slings and double-head slings built to hang blocks and choke heavy wood.
intro: A heavy duty sling handles the large, dynamic loads of removals where big wood is being lowered. These dead-eye, bull rope and double-head rigging slings anchor blocks and choke heavy pieces.

p: A dead-eye sling has one spliced eye and a tail. Pass the tail around the stem and through the eye to choke it, or tie a knot to the rope. They grip stems well and pass easily through crotches. A larger diameter dead-eye spreads load on bark and handles heavier pieces.

Dead-eye slings come in several diameters and lengths. A thicker sling holds blocks for larger removals and is less likely to cut into soft bark. A thinner, shorter one is quicker to set on small limbs and pieces being lowered. Many arborists keep a range so they can pick the right one at the tie-in.

Bull rope rigging slings are made from heavy rigging rope and are built to hang blocks for big removals. Double-head slings have an eye at each end, so you can basket or choke them around a stem and clip both eyes to the block.
The sling holding the block often sees the highest load in the system, so it should be at least as strong as the block and rope. Wrap it on solid wood below the block's attachment point.

Some crews prefer a sling with a protective sleeve where it wraps the trunk to reduce wear. Others use a cambium saver or ring setup to protect the bark. Choose what works for your trees and your rigging style, but keep the rating of the sling in mind first.

Choose diameter and length based on the stems you work and the loads you plan to lower. Too short and you cannot wrap the stem; too long and the block hangs low and swings. Many crews carry a few sizes.

Trad slings and loop runners also have their place for lighter rigging and redirects. For heavy-duty rigging and big removals, stronger rope slings with spliced eyes and a large diameter are a safer bet. Choose length so the block hangs close to the stem and the rope runs cleanly.

Double-head rigging slings are popular for hanging blocks on large stems because the two eyes clip together on the block, spreading load evenly. Long double-head slings, such as 25 feet or so, can wrap big trunks with room to spare, which is useful on large removals and crane-assisted jobs.

Look for cuts, glazing, abrasion and damaged splices before each use. Replace slings that have been shock loaded heavily or show damage, and keep them away from saw chains and sharp edges. Follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

Keep a record of when each heavy sling went into service and any severe shock loads it has taken. That history helps decide when to retire it. Damaged splices, a hardened or glazed section, or core damage are clear signs to take a sling out of service.

faq.q: What is a dead-eye sling used for?
faq.a: It chokes stems to hang blocks or attach pieces being lowered, with one eye and a free tail.

faq.q: How strong should a block sling be?
faq.a: At least as strong as the block and rope it supports, with margin for dynamic loads.

faq.q: Can I splice my own heavy duty sling?
faq.a: Only if you are trained in the splice for that rope and test your work. Otherwise, buy professionally made slings.

faq.q: How do I protect heavy slings from wear?
faq.a: Keep them clean, out of the saw's path and off sharp edges, and rotate how they are set so wear is spread.

name: Rope
h1: Arborist Rope for Climbing and Rigging
title: Arborist Rope: Climbing, Rigging & Hitch Cord
meta: Arborist rope for climbing and rigging: 16-strand, 24-strand and static climbing lines, rigging rope, hitch cord and splicing gear, with tips on choosing.
intro: Arborist rope is the most important gear decision a climber makes and the backbone of every rigging system. This arborist supply department covers climbing rope, rigging rope, tech cordage for hitches, and the rope accessories that keep lines in service.

p: Climbing rope is life-support gear. It is built for consistent handling with friction hitches and mechanical devices, low stretch for efficient ascents, and strength well above body-weight loads. Arborist climbing lines typically run from about 11 mm to 13 mm, and the climbing system you use determines what will work.

Rigging rope is made to absorb and control the shock of lowering wood. It is usually larger, commonly 1/2 inch to 3/4 inch, with high strength and some stretch to soften dynamic loads. Never use a rigging line as a climbing line, and retire any climbing line that has been used for rigging.

Climbing rope and rigging rope also look and handle differently. Many crews choose bright, distinctive colors for climbing lines and solid colors for rigging lines, so nobody grabs the wrong rope from the truck. Label rope bags clearly and store the two types apart.

Sixteen-strand ropes have a tough, thick cover over a lightly twisted core. They are proven, durable and grip well with traditional friction hitches like the Blake's hitch. Twenty-four strand and other modern constructions use a tighter, rounder cover that runs smoothly through mechanical devices and hitches, and many are popular for stationary rope systems.

Static and low-stretch kernmantle ropes have little elongation, which suits SRS ascents and devices built around specific diameters. Always check that your rope is listed as compatible in your device's instructions.

guide.h: Picking the right diameter and length
p: Your diameter is set by your hitch cord and devices. Too thin and a hitch may not grab; too thick and it will drag. Length depends on the trees you climb: you need at least twice the height of your highest tie-in point for a doubled rope technique, plus extra for redirects and safety. Many climbers buy 150 or 200 feet and cut shorter lines from worn rope as it ages.
For rigging rope, diameter and strength depend on the loads you lower. Size up when in doubt and plan cuts to limit shock loading.

If you are buying from a rope store or rope supply for the first time, start with one climbing line and one rigging line, a few lengths of hitch cord and a chafe sleeve. Add specialized ropes like static lines for SRS as your system grows.

Inspect rope before each climb: run it through your hands looking for cuts, glazing, flat or stiff spots, core damage and contamination. Keep it out of the saw's path, away from fuel and chemicals, and store it clean and dry in a rope bag. Follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions for life-support rope, and retire it when in doubt. A climbing line costs less than a fall.

Splicing tools, chafe sleeves and hitch cord are part of a rope kit, too. A chafe sleeve protects a rope where it passes over bark or edges, and good hitch cord matched to your line keeps your system working smoothly.

Keep a simple log for each life-support rope: date in service, inspections and any events like a shock load or saw contact. That record makes retirement decisions easier and helps if anyone ever asks how your gear is managed.

faq.q: What is the best arborist rope for a beginner?
faq.a: A reputable 16-strand or 24-strand climbing line in the diameter your hitch cord and devices are rated for. Get trained on that system before you climb.

faq.q: Can I use rigging rope for climbing?
faq.a: No. Rigging rope is not designed or rated as life-support gear for climbing, and a climbing line used for rigging should be retired from climbing.

faq.q: How long does a climbing rope last?
faq.a: It depends on use, storage and damage. Inspect it before every climb and retire it whenever damage or doubt appears, following the manufacturer's guidance.

faq.q: What diameter climbing rope should I buy?
faq.a: Choose the diameter your hitch cord, ascenders and friction devices are rated for. Most arborist lines fall roughly between 11 mm and 13 mm.

name: Climbing Rope
title: Tree Climbing Rope: Arborist Climbing Lines by Type
meta: Tree climbing rope for arborists: 16-strand, 24-strand and static climbing lines, plus a rope placement tool, with tips on diameter, length and inspection.
intro: Tree climbing rope is life-support gear, so it is worth choosing carefully. Arborist climbing rope comes in 16-strand, 24-strand and static constructions, each with its own feel with hitches and devices.

p: Start with your system. Traditional doubled-rope climbing with a friction hitch works well with 16-strand rope. Mechanical devices and SRS often favor a round, firm 24-strand or static line in a specific diameter. Check your devices' instructions for compatible ropes.

Length should be at least twice your highest tie-in for doubled rope, with extra to spare. Inspect before every climb, keep the rope away from saws and fuel, and follow ANSI Z133 and the maker's instructions. Get trained before you climb.

Sixteen-strand ropes have thick covers that resist abrasion and play well with traditional friction hitches. Twenty-four strand ropes are round and firm, which suits devices and SRS. Static lines have the least stretch for efficient rope ascents and are common in stationary systems.

Rope accessories round out a climbing kit: a throw line and weight to set your rope, a rope bag to store it, a chafe sleeve for rough tie-ins and a rope placement tool for reaching high anchors from the ground. Build your system as a whole so every part is compatible.

faq.q: How long should my tree climbing rope be?
faq.a: For a doubled rope system you need at least twice your tie-in height, plus extra. Many climbers start with 150 feet.

name: 16-Strand Rope
title: 16-Strand Climbing Rope for Tree Climbers
meta: 16-strand climbing rope for arborists: durable, hitch-friendly classic climbing lines with a thick cover that handles bark, friction hitches and daily use.
intro: A 16-strand climbing rope has a heavy cover braided from 16 strands over a lightly twisted core. It is a classic arborist line, durable and easy to grip with traditional friction hitches.

p: The thick cover stands up to bark and abrasion, and the rope tends to be forgiving with hitches like the Blake's hitch. It is a solid choice for doubled-rope climbing and new climbers learning a traditional system.

Some 16-strand ropes are a little stiffer or have more stretch than modern constructions, which can matter on SRS devices. Confirm compatibility with your gear and inspect the rope before every climb.

A 16-strand cover will fuzz with use, which is normal. What is not normal is a glazed, stiff or flat section, exposed core, or any cut through the cover. Run the rope through your hands before every climb and retire it if you find damage or are unsure.

Store the rope clean and dry in a rope bag out of sunlight, and keep it away from fuel, oils and chemicals. Many climbers mark their lines with the date in service and keep a simple log. Follow the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 for life-support rope.

faq.q: Is 16-strand rope good for SRS?
faq.a: Some climbers use it, but many SRS devices are designed for specific rope types and diameters. Check the device instructions first.

name: 24-Strand Rope
title: 24-Strand Climbing Rope: Smooth Lines for Devices
meta: 24-strand climbing rope for arborists: round, firm climbing lines in about 11.7 to 12.5 mm that run smoothly through mechanical devices and friction hitches.
intro: A 24-strand climbing rope uses a tighter cover braid that keeps the rope round and firm. That smooth, consistent feel is why many climbers choose 24-strand line for mechanical devices and SRS.

p: Twenty-four strand ropes tend to run smoothly through devices and resist flattening, which makes ascents and descents more predictable. Pay attention to diameter, because a few tenths of a millimeter can change how a hitch or device grips.
As with any life-support rope, check compatibility with your hitch cord and devices, inspect before every climb and follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

Common 24-strand arborist lines run from about 11.7 mm to 12.5 mm. A slightly thinner line saves weight and runs faster through devices; a slightly thicker one gives more grip and wear life. Many devices list specific diameter ranges, so start there.

Inspect before each climb for cuts, glazing, core damage and contamination, and store the rope clean and dry. Retire it when in doubt. A bright color helps the ground crew see where your line is in the canopy, which is a real safety bonus during rigging.

faq.q: Is 24-strand rope better than 16-strand?
faq.a: Neither is better for everyone. 24-strand often suits devices and SRS; 16-strand is durable and hitch-friendly for traditional climbing.

name: Static Rope
title: Static Climbing Rope: Low-Stretch Arborist Lines
meta: Static climbing rope for arborists: low-stretch kernmantle lines such as Sterling HTP 11mm and WorkPro 12.5mm for SRS ascents and mechanical devices.
intro: Static climbing rope stretches very little, so more of your effort goes into moving up instead of stretching the line. Static arborist rope is popular for SRS ascents and work positioning.

p: Kernmantle static lines have a protective sheath over a load-bearing core. Diameters such as 11 mm and 12.5 mm are common, and the right one depends on your devices. Thinner lines are lighter; thicker lines are easier to grip and wear longer.

Static rope has little ability to absorb a fall, so it must never be used where a climber could fall onto it with slack. Use it within the device maker's listed ropes, inspect before every climb, and get trained on SRS before using it.

Stationary rope systems put all the wear in one spot on the anchor, so use a friction saver or rope protector where needed and move the anchor point as wear appears. Rope ends see a lot of handling; terminate them with a sewn or spliced eye or an approved knot.

Low-stretch lines like Sterling HTP and WorkPro are popular with arborists for SRS, while some climbers prefer a static line with a softer hand. Whatever you choose, read the device and rope instructions, check compatibility, and train on SRS before you rely on it.

faq.q: Can I climb on any static rope?
faq.a: Use a rope intended for life support and listed as compatible with your devices. Not every static rope is suited to arborist systems.

name: Rigging Rope
title: Tree Rigging Rope: Rigging Line in 1/2 to 3/4 Inch
meta: Tree rigging rope for lowering wood: double-braid and stable braid rigging line in 1/2, 5/8 and 3/4 inch for blocks, lowering devices and removals.
intro: Tree rigging rope takes the shock of lowering wood, so it needs high strength and some stretch. These rigging ropes come in 1/2, 5/8 and 3/4 inch diameters.

p: Size by the loads you lower and the blocks and lowering devices you use. A 1/2 inch line is good for lighter pruning and small removals, while 5/8 and 3/4 inch handle bigger wood. Double-braid ropes are strong and absorb shock; firmer braids hold shape on blocks.
Keep rigging rope separate from climbing rope, inspect it for cuts and glazing, and retire it after severe shock loads or damage.

Rigging rope takes repeated shock loading and abrasion. Look for glazing, flat spots, cuts, pulled strands and hard or crunchy sections that point to core damage. Severe shock loads can damage rope internally even when it looks fine on the outside, so retire rope after a big dynamic event.

Keep rigging lines away from the saw, use a chafe sleeve over rough bark, and store rope clean and dry. Label rigging and climbing ropes clearly so they never get mixed. Order ahead so a spare rigging line is on the truck before the current one needs replacing.

faq.q: What size rigging rope should I buy first?
faq.a: Many crews start with 1/2 or 5/8 inch, matched to their block and lowering device.

name: Rope Care
h1: Rope Splicing Tools and Rope Care
title: Rope Splicing Tools & Rope Care: Chafe Sleeves
meta: Rope splicing tools and rope care gear for arborists: heavy-duty chafe sleeves that protect climbing and rigging lines, plus notes on splicing and storage.
intro: Rope splicing tools and rope care gear protect your investment in climbing and rigging lines. Chafe sleeves cover rope where it runs over bark or edges.

p: A chafe sleeve slides over a rope at a friction point, such as a crotch or edge, to cut abrasion. Heavy-duty sleeves last longer on rough bark and rigging lines.

Splicing tools such as fids and pushers let trained users make eyes and terminations. Only splice life-support rope if you are trained in that splice for that rope, and follow the rope maker's instructions. Store rope clean and dry, away from fuel and sunlight.

A rope splicing kit typically includes hollow fids sized to rope diameters, a pusher, a marker and measuring tape. Different rope constructions use different splices, so the rope maker's splicing instructions are the place to start.

Splicing your own rigging slings, eye-to-eye prusiks and rope ends can save money and give you a custom fit, but only with proper training and testing. Many arborists send life-support splices to a professional splicer. Good tools for rope work make clean, tidy splices that hold up and run well through hardware.

faq.q: Do I need a chafe sleeve?
faq.a: It is worth carrying, especially for rigging and when your line runs over rough bark or edges.

name: Tech Cordage
title: Hitch Cord & Tech Cordage by the Foot
meta: Hitch cord and tech cordage by the foot for arborists: friction hitch cord for climbing systems, ring rope for friction savers and shock cord for gear.
intro: Hitch cord is what turns a rope into a climbing system. This tech cordage is sold by the foot, so you can cut friction hitches, ring rope and shock cord to length.

p: Pick hitch cord in a diameter and stiffness that grips your climbing line. Thinner cord grabs more, thicker cord runs smoother. Ring rope is used to build friction savers and adjustable anchors. Shock cord is for gear organization, not life support.
Tie or splice hitches only if you have been trained to, test them low before climbing, and replace hitch cord at the first sign of glazing or wear.

Hitch cord works hard, absorbs heat and wears faster than your climbing line. Check it before every climb for glazing, stiffness, cuts and core damage, and replace it often. Keep spare lengths in your kit so a worn hitch does not cut your day short.

Ring rope for friction savers should be inspected like any life-support component. Shock cord is great for holding gear and tool lanyards but is never part of a climbing system. Store cordage clean, dry and out of sunlight.

faq.q: How long should a hitch cord be?
faq.a: It depends on the hitch and your setup. Follow the guidance for the hitch you tie and your trainer's advice.

name: Safety
title: Arborist Safety Gear: Helmets, PPE & First Aid
meta: Arborist safety gear for tree crews: helmets, eye and hearing protection, chainsaw protection, gloves, first aid, fall protection and traffic control.
intro: Arborist safety gear is the part of the kit you hope never gets tested. This department covers helmets, eye and hearing protection, gloves, chainsaw protection, first aid, fall protection, communication and traffic control.

p: A helmet built for tree work protects against falling debris and impacts, and many climbers choose helmets that meet climbing and industrial standards. Pair it with a mesh or clear visor and safety glasses rated to ANSI Z87.1, and with helmet-mounted ear muffs. Chainsaws and chippers are loud enough to damage hearing over time, so hearing protection is not optional.
Communication headsets let climbers and ground crew talk without shouting over saws, which cuts down on mistakes during rigging.

Helmets have a service life set by the manufacturer. Replace a helmet after a significant impact, when the shell is cracked or faded, or when the suspension is damaged. Keep the visor, ear muffs and chin strap in good repair, because a helmet that is uncomfortable or broken tends to come off on the job.

Gloves protect against cuts, splinters and rope burns; choose snug, dexterous gloves for climbing and tougher ones for brush. Chaps or chainsaw pants protect legs during ground saw work, and sturdy boots with good support finish the kit.

Gloves and boots are personal fit items, so let crew members try sizes before buying in bulk. For saw work on the ground, ANSI Z133 expects chain-saw-resistant leg protection. Many crews standardize on chaps for shared use and offer chainsaw pants to full-time saw operators.

Every truck needs a stocked first-aid kit that includes bleeding control supplies, and crews need people trained to use it. Aerial rescue plans and practice are part of being ready, too. Rescue training mannequins let crews practice aerial rescue without risk.

Write down your emergency plan for each job: the address, the nearest hospital, who calls 911, who handles aerial rescue and where the first-aid kit is. Go over it in the tailgate briefing before work starts. It takes a few minutes and pays off when something goes wrong.

Rescue preparedness is part of the safety kit. Every crew with a climber aloft should have someone on the ground trained and equipped to perform an aerial rescue, with a plan agreed before the climb. Practice the plan on a regular schedule so it works under stress.

Cones, signs and high-visibility vests define the work zone and protect crews working near roads and sidewalks. Follow the MUTCD and local rules for work zones along roadways. ANSI Z133 sets out PPE and work-zone expectations for arboricultural operations, so read the current edition and match your company's policy to it.

Arborist safety gear works best as a system. A helmet with a visor and ear muffs, a communication headset, gloves, chaps, boots and a vest can all be fitted together so nothing interferes with anything else. Review your crew's PPE every season and replace worn items before they fail.

faq.q: What safety gear does an arborist need?
faq.a: At minimum: a helmet, eye protection, hearing protection, gloves, appropriate footwear, leg protection for ground saw work and a stocked first-aid kit, plus training.

faq.q: Do arborist helmets need to meet a standard?
faq.a: Yes. Choose helmets that meet the standards required by ANSI Z133 and your employer, such as ANSI Z89.1.

faq.q: How often should safety gear be replaced?
faq.a: Follow manufacturer service-life guidance, and replace anything that has been damaged, impacted or degraded.

faq.q: Is first-aid training required for tree crews?
faq.a: ANSI Z133 and OSHA expect trained people and first-aid supplies at the work site. Check the current rules for your situation.

name: Communication
title: Arborist Communication System: Bluetooth Helmet Headsets
meta: Arborist communication system options: Bluetooth helmet headsets, mesh intercom and FRS radio ear muffs that let climbers and ground crews talk over saws.
intro: An arborist communication system lets the climber and ground crew talk clearly over saws and chippers. Choose a Bluetooth helmet headset with mesh intercom, an integrated helmet system or radio ear muffs.

p: Rigging, felling and aerial rescue all depend on clear commands. Hand signals and shouting work until a chipper is running or the climber is out of sight. A headset on each helmet lets the crew confirm commands like stand clear, ready to cut and let it run before anything moves.
Many crews still use a clear call-and-response system, even with headsets. Communication gear supports good procedures; it does not replace them.

Communication also helps ground crew warn the climber about hazards they cannot see from above, such as a car pulling into the drop zone, a pedestrian on the sidewalk or a rope fouled on a fence. That shared awareness is one of the biggest safety benefits of a headset system.

Bluetooth headsets pair directly between a few users. Mesh intercom systems connect multiple helmets in a group without pairing each one, and they handle people moving in and out of range more gracefully. Look at range, group size and battery life for a full day.

Range and battery life vary between systems. Check the manufacturer's stated figures, but expect real-world range to be lower among trees, buildings and running equipment. Charge every unit overnight and keep a charging cable in the truck.

guide.h: Integrated helmet systems and radio muffs
p: An integrated arborist helmet with Bluetooth or a communication kit built for a specific helmet keeps cables tidy and puts speakers inside hearing protection. Radio ear muffs with FRS radios work across mixed crews and longer distances where licensed or license-free radio channels apply.
Make sure the system's ear cups still provide the hearing protection your crew needs, and keep volume at levels that do not add noise exposure.

Some arborist helmets offer a dedicated communication kit designed to fit their shell and ear muffs. These kits often give the cleanest install and the best audio quality. Check whether your helmet maker offers one before choosing an aftermarket system.
Check compatibility with your helmets before buying, think about how many people need to talk at once, and plan for charging. Test the system at the start of each day.

Train every crew member on the system's controls, especially how to mute, change volume and reconnect. A headset that only one person knows how to use will not help in an emergency. Set agreed-upon call signs and commands so everyone knows who is speaking and what the call means.

Plan for weather, too. Many systems handle light rain, but check the manufacturer's water resistance rating before working in heavy rain. Keep spare batteries or a power bank in the truck, and mark each headset with a crew member's name so units do not get swapped between helmets with different settings.

faq.q: Can I add communication to my existing arborist helmet?
faq.a: Many systems mount to popular helmets or their ear muffs. Check the compatibility list before you buy.

faq.q: How many people can share a mesh intercom?
faq.a: It depends on the system. Mesh intercoms are designed for groups larger than Bluetooth pairing allows.

faq.q: Do communication headsets provide hearing protection?
faq.a: Some systems are built into rated ear muffs. Others are speakers only, so pair them with proper hearing protection.

faq.q: Do headsets replace hand signals?
faq.a: No. Keep a backup system of signals and clear commands.

name: Eye Protection
h1: Eye Visor and Arborist Eye Protection
title: Eye Visor & Arborist Eye Protection
meta: Eye visor and eye protection for arborists: mesh and clear helmet visors for Kask and Petzl helmets plus ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses for saw and chipper work.
intro: A helmet-mounted eye visor keeps chips and sawdust out of your face while you work. Pair it with safety glasses, since a mesh visor alone will not stop fine particles.

p: Mesh visors breathe well and do not fog, but fine dust and small particles can pass through. Clear visors block more debris but can fog and scratch. Many arborists wear safety glasses under a visor for full protection.
Pick a visor made for your helmet model, and safety glasses marked ANSI Z87.1. Replace scratched lenses and damaged visors so your vision stays clear.

Mesh visors are popular for saw work because they do not fog and let air through. Clear polycarbonate visors offer more coverage against fine dust and chips. Visors come in different lengths; a longer visor protects more of the face but can get in the way when looking up.

Make sure the visor fits your helmet model or uses an approved adapter. Combine it with safety glasses, keep spare lenses on the truck, and clean visors with water and a soft cloth to avoid scratches.

faq.q: Is a mesh visor enough eye protection?
faq.a: Typically no. Wear ANSI Z87.1 safety glasses as primary eye protection and use the visor for extra face coverage.

name: Fall Protection
h1: Fall Protection Equipment and Rescue Gear
title: Fall Protection Equipment & Rescue Training Gear
meta: Fall protection equipment for tree crews: full-body harnesses for aerial lifts and rope access and rescue training dummies for practicing aerial rescue.
intro: Fall protection equipment covers the harnesses and rescue gear used in aerial lifts and work at height. A full-body harness and a rescue dummy for training round out a crew's readiness.

p: Full-body harnesses are used in aerial lifts and some rope access work where fall arrest is required. They are different from tree climbing saddles, so follow the lift and harness maker's instructions on which to use. Fit the harness snugly and inspect webbing, stitching and buckles before each use.

A rescue training mannequin lets crews practice aerial rescue at realistic weight without putting a person at risk. Regular practice with a qualified trainer is the best fall rescue equipment you can have.

Fall protection is only as good as the people using it. Anyone in an aerial lift or working at height should be trained on harness fit, anchorage and the lift manufacturer's requirements. Crews should practice aerial rescue on a regular schedule with a qualified trainer.

Inspect harnesses before each use, look for cuts, burns, broken stitching and damaged hardware, and retire any harness that has arrested a fall. Store fall protection clean and dry and away from chemicals. Follow ANSI Z133 and the equipment manufacturer's instructions.

faq.q: Is a full-body harness the same as a climbing saddle?
faq.a: No. They serve different purposes and are built to different standards. Use the one required for the work you are doing.

name: First Aid
h1: Arborist First Aid Kits and Bleeding Control
title: Arborist First Aid Kit: Trauma & Bleeding Control
meta: Arborist first aid kit supplies for chainsaw and logging crews: hemostatic gauze, bleeding control gear and what a crew kit should hold under ANSI Z133.
intro: An arborist first aid kit has to handle more than scrapes and splinters. Chainsaws, chippers and falling wood can cause serious bleeding, so a crew kit for tree work or logging needs trauma and bleeding control supplies alongside everyday first aid, and people trained to use them.

guide.h: Why tree crews need a trauma-ready kit
p: Most job site injuries are minor: cuts, splinters, eye irritation, stings. The ones that matter most are rarer and faster: a chainsaw cut to the leg or arm, a chipper injury, or a crushing injury from falling wood. Severe bleeding can become life-threatening in minutes, often before an ambulance can reach a rural or backyard job site.

That is why many arborists and loggers add bleeding control supplies, often called a chainsaw first aid kit or forestry first aid kit, to the standard workplace kit. Carry one on every truck and keep a small personal kit on the climber or the saw operator.

The time between injury and professional care is what makes tree work different. A backyard removal may be minutes from an ambulance; a right-of-way job or woodlot may be much further. Plan your kit and training for the job site you are actually on.

guide.h: What a crew kit should hold
p: Start from a workplace first-aid kit that meets ANSI/ISEA Z308.1, then add for the hazards of tree work. Bleeding control: a commercial tourniquet of a type taught in recognized courses, hemostatic gauze, pressure or emergency trauma bandages, and plenty of gauze for packing and dressing. Basics: nitrile gloves, trauma shears, adhesive bandages, tape, antiseptic wipes, burn dressings, eye wash and splinter tweezers.

Add a CPR face shield, an emergency blanket, cold packs and a card with the job address and nearest hospital. Crews with members who have known severe allergies should follow that person's own medical plan. Check expiration dates and restock after every use.

Pack the kit in a bright, weather-resistant bag or case so it is easy to find and protected from fuel, sawdust and rain. Separate bleeding control supplies into their own clearly labeled pouch so nobody has to dig through bandages in an emergency.

ANSI Z133 expects first-aid supplies at the job site and crew members trained in first aid and CPR, and OSHA requires trained responders and adequate supplies where medical care is not close by. Read the current edition and your state rules for the exact wording, because requirements change.

Supplies only help in trained hands. We strongly recommend a recognized first aid and CPR course for everyone on the crew, plus a bleeding control course such as Stop the Bleed. Practice applying a tourniquet and packing a wound on a trainer, not for the first time on a coworker. This page is not medical advice; follow your training and call emergency services right away for serious injuries.

Mount the kit where everyone knows it lives, in the same spot on every truck. Keep a tourniquet and hemostatic gauze where they can be reached in seconds, not buried under bandages. Check the kit weekly, replace anything used or expired, and include it in your tailgate safety briefing and aerial rescue drills.

Make sure everyone on the crew knows the address of the job, has a phone with signal or a radio, and knows who will meet the ambulance at the street. Small details like that save minutes when they count.

faq.q: What should be in an arborist first aid kit?
faq.a: A standard workplace kit plus bleeding control supplies: a tourniquet, hemostatic gauze, pressure bandages, gloves and shears, along with burn, eye and basic wound care items.

faq.q: Does ANSI Z133 require first-aid training?
faq.a: Z133 expects first-aid supplies at the work site and trained crew members, including CPR. Check the current edition and your employer's policy for exact requirements.

faq.q: Is hemostatic gauze safe to use?
faq.a: It is widely used for severe bleeding when applied as taught in a bleeding control course. Get trained before relying on it and follow the product instructions.

faq.q: How is a logger first aid kit different from a regular kit?
faq.a: It adds trauma supplies for severe bleeding and is built to survive a truck or the woods, since help may be far away.

name: Gloves
title: Arborist Gloves: Tree Climbing & Saw Work Gloves
meta: Arborist gloves for climbing, rigging and saw work: snug, grippy tree climbing gloves and tough technical gloves that protect hands while keeping dexterity.
intro: Arborist gloves need to grip rope and saws while protecting against splinters, abrasion and rope burn. Tree climbing gloves trade some armor for dexterity; work gloves for brush and chipping trade the other way.

p: For climbing, look for a snug fit, good grip when wet and enough feel to tie knots and handle carabiners. For ground work and chipping, choose tougher palms and longer cuffs. Nitrile-coated gloves are a cheap, grippy option many crews buy by the pack.
Never wear loose gloves near chippers or other machinery with infeed or rotating parts. Replace gloves with holes in the palm or fingertips.

Rinse grime out of leather gloves and let them dry slowly away from direct heat to keep them soft. Synthetic gloves can usually be washed. Replace gloves with worn-through palms, split seams or holes, since splinters and rope burns find those first.

Many climbers carry two pairs: a thin, grippy pair for climbing and tying knots and a tougher pair for rigging, chipping and hauling brush. Gloves that fit well get worn, and gloves that fit poorly end up in the truck. Try different sizes before buying a stock for the crew.

faq.q: Are chainsaw gloves necessary?
faq.a: Some gloves include cut protection on the back of the hand. Requirements vary, so follow your employer's PPE policy.

name: Hearing Protection
h1: Helmet Ear Muffs and Hearing Protection
title: Helmet Ear Muffs & Helmet Ear Protection
meta: Helmet ear muffs and helmet ear protection for arborists: clip-on muffs for climbing helmets, replacement hygiene kits and tips on fit and noise ratings.
intro: Helmet ear muffs clip to your helmet so hearing protection is always there when the saw starts. This helmet ear protection works with common arborist helmets and swings up when you need to talk.

p: Chainsaws, chippers and stump grinders are loud enough to cause permanent hearing loss over time. Damage builds up slowly and does not come back. ANSI Z133 and OSHA both address hearing protection for noisy work, and the simplest way to comply is protection mounted on the helmet so it is never left in the truck.

Noise-induced hearing loss is one of the most common occupational injuries, and tree crews are exposed to it every day. Ringing in the ears after work is a warning sign. Wearing protection the whole time equipment is running, not just during the loudest cuts, is what prevents long-term damage.

Check that the muffs fit your helmet's slots or mounting system. Noise reduction ratings help compare models, but a good seal matters more than the number on the box. Hair, glasses and worn cushions break the seal.
Some muffs have built-in radio or Bluetooth for a communication system. Make sure those still provide adequate protection and keep volume moderate.

Ear muff and helmet combinations from the same manufacturer are often the easiest to set up and give the best fit. If your helmet uses a universal slot system, aftermarket muffs may also fit. Make sure the muffs can be swung up and parked without falling off when you need to talk with the crew.

Helmet ear muffs should press evenly around the ear without gaps. Adjust the mounting arms so the cups sit centered over your ears, and check the seal each time you put the helmet on. Muffs with worn springs or loose arms should be replaced, since they no longer press firmly enough to seal.

Ear cushions and foam inserts harden and crack with sweat and sun. Replace them with the maker's hygiene kit at least once or twice a year or when they no longer seal. It is the cheapest way to restore performance.

Clean cushions and the inside of the cups with a damp cloth and mild soap, and let them dry before storing. Do not soak ear muffs in water or use solvents on them. Store helmets with muffs out of direct sun so plastics and foam last longer.
Foam or reusable earplugs are a good backup and can be combined with muffs for very loud work. Insert them correctly for them to work.

Ear protection helmet setups work best when everyone on the crew wears them consistently. Make hearing protection part of the standard PPE check at the start of each job, alongside helmets, eye protection and chaps. Annual hearing tests help catch changes early, and many employers provide them.
Keep a box of disposable foam earplugs on the truck for visitors, new crew members and anyone whose muffs are damaged, so nobody works near running equipment unprotected.

faq.q: Will any ear muff fit my helmet?
faq.a: No. Helmet ear muffs use specific mounts. Check compatibility with your helmet model.

faq.q: How often should I replace ear muff cushions?
faq.a: Commonly every six months to a year with regular use, or sooner if they crack or stop sealing.

faq.q: Are helmet ear muffs as good as headband muffs?
faq.a: They can be, when fitted correctly. Compare noise ratings and check the seal.

faq.q: Can I wear earplugs and ear muffs together?
faq.a: Yes, for very loud work. It increases protection, though not by the full sum of both ratings.

name: Traffic Control
h1: Traffic Control Gear for Tree Crews
title: Traffic Control Gear: Cones, Signs & Hi-Viz Vests
meta: Traffic control gear for tree crews working near roads: drop zone cones, tree work ahead signs and Class 2 hi-viz safety vests to mark your work zone.
intro: Traffic control gear marks the work zone and keeps crews, drivers and pedestrians apart. Cones, signs and high-visibility vests are the basics for any job near a road or sidewalk.

p: Use signs to warn drivers before they reach the work area, cones to define the drop zone and lane closures, and Class 2 or higher vests for anyone working near traffic. Mark the drop zone on residential jobs too, so homeowners and passers-by stay clear.
Work zones on public roads must follow the MUTCD and local permit rules. Train flaggers and plan setup before the first cut.

A basic tree crew traffic kit includes advance warning signs, enough cones to taper and close a lane, high-visibility vests for everyone, flagger paddles where flagging is needed and drop zone cones for the work area. Keep it on the truck so it is used every time.

Replace signs and cones that are faded, cracked or have lost reflective sheeting, and keep vests clean so they stay bright. Check with the road authority about permits, lane closure layouts and any local rules for night or high-speed roads.

faq.q: What vest class do tree workers need near roads?
faq.a: Many roadside jobs call for ANSI/ISEA 107 Class 2 or higher. Check the requirements for your road and jurisdiction.

Climbing rope, connectors and other life-support equipment must meet the applicable standards and be used according to ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions. Inspect it before every use and retire it when damaged or in doubt. If you are new to climbing, get trained before you buy a full kit, since your trainer will help decide what system suits you.

Rigging equipment also needs to be matched and rated for the loads you plan to lower. Read the rated strength of every component, keep rigging gear separate from life-support gear and inspect everything before each job. Training with a qualified instructor is the best way to learn rigging safely.

name: Featured Gear
title: Featured Arborist Gear: Throw Line, Rope & Pullers
meta: Featured arborist gear picks: throw line for setting ropes, static rope hanks, chainsaw pants and a continuous rope puller kit for tree crews and climbers.
intro: Featured arborist gear is a short list of tools worth a look: throw line for setting climbing lines, short static rope hanks, chainsaw pants and a continuous rope puller kit.

p: Throw line and a throw weight set your climbing line in the canopy, and a thin, slick line with a bright color is easiest to manage. Short static rope hanks are handy for lanyards, anchors and practice systems. A continuous rope puller makes pulling trees and tensioning lines easier, and chainsaw pants protect the saw operator all day.
Check compatibility and ratings for anything used as life support or rigging, and follow ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions.

These picks come from different departments, so use them as a quick start, then visit the category pages for the full selection and buying guides. Product pages show a typical price and a Check price button for current pricing and availability.

Throw line pairs with a throw weight and line storage bag. Static rope hanks pair with hardware rated for the use. The continuous rope puller pairs with a rated anchor sling. Chainsaw pants pair with good boots and a helmet system. Building a kit as a system saves money and keeps everything compatible.

faq.q: What throw line should I start with?
faq.a: A slick, bright, mid-diameter throw line pairs with a common throw weight for most climbers. Practice your throws before relying on it on a job.
